```python
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import hashlib
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any, Dict, List, Mapping, Optional


SCHEMA_VERSION = "1.0"
ARTIFACT_TYPE = "execution_result_record"


# =========================
# Deterministic Utilities
# =========================

def _canonicalize(obj: Any) -> Any:
    """
    Recursively canonicalize data into a deterministic structure.
    - Sort dict keys
    - Ensure lists are canonicalized element-wise
    """
    if isinstance(obj, Mapping):
        return {k: _canonicalize(obj[k]) for k in sorted(obj.keys())}
    elif isinstance(obj, list):
        return [_canonicalize(v) for v in obj]
    else:
        return obj


def _canonical_json(obj: Any) -> str:
    return json.dumps(_canonicalize(obj), separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=False)


def make_execution_result_id(payload: Mapping[str, Any]) -> str:
    """
    Deterministic ID based on canonicalized payload (excluding ID field itself).
    """
    canonical = _canonical_json(payload)
    digest = hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
    return f"execution_result_{digest}"


# =========================
# Validation
# =========================

_ALLOWED_PLAN_STATUS = {"SUCCEEDED", "PARTIAL", "FAILED", "SKIPPED"}
_ALLOWED_STEP_STATUS = {"SUCCEEDED", "FAILED", "SKIPPED"}


def _require(condition: bool, message: str) -> None:
    if not condition:
        raise ValueError(message)


def _validate_mapping(name: str, value: Any) -> None:
    _require(isinstance(value, Mapping), f"{name} must be a mapping")


def _validate_optional_mapping(name: str, value: Any) -> None:
    if value is not None:
        _validate_mapping(name, value)


def _validate_step_result(step: Mapping[str, Any], index: int) -> None:
    required_fields = {
        "step_index",
        "step_id",
        "action_type",
        "status",
        "input_payload",
        "output_payload",
        "error",
    }

    _validate_mapping("step_result", step)

    missing = required_fields - set(step.keys())
    _require(not missing, f"step_result[{index}] missing fields: {missing}")

    _require(step["step_index"] == index, "step_index must match list position")

    _require(
        step["status"] in _ALLOWED_STEP_STATUS,
        f"Invalid step status: {step['status']}"
    )

    _validate_mapping("input_payload", step["input_payload"])
    _validate_optional_mapping("output_payload", step["output_payload"])

    error = step["error"]
    if error is not None:
        _validate_mapping("error", error)
        _require("error_type" in error, "error missing error_type")
        _require("message" in error, "error missing message")


def _validate_execution_status(value: str) -> None:
    _require(value in _ALLOWED_PLAN_STATUS, f"Invalid execution_status: {value}")


# =========================
# Core Artifact
# =========================

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionResultRecord:
    schema_version: str
    execution_result_record_id: str
    artifact_type: str

    authority: Mapping[str, Any]
    evidence: Mapping[str, Any]
    determinism: Mapping[str, Any]

    plan_record_id: str
    decision_record_id: str
    subject_id: str

    execution_status: str
    step_results: List[Mapping[str, Any]]
    summary: Mapping[str, Any]

    rationale: Optional[str] = None
    emitted_by: Optional[str] = None

    # -------------------------
    # Validation
    # -------------------------

    def __post_init__(self):
        _require(self.schema_version == SCHEMA_VERSION, "Invalid schema_version")
        _require(self.artifact_type == ARTIFACT_TYPE, "Invalid artifact_type")

        _validate_mapping("authority", self.authority)
        _validate_mapping("evidence", self.evidence)
        _validate_mapping("determinism", self.determinism)

        _require(self.plan_record_id, "plan_record_id required")
        _require(self.decision_record_id, "decision_record_id required")
        _require(self.subject_id, "subject_id required")

        _validate_execution_status(self.execution_status)

        _require(isinstance(self.step_results, list), "step_results must be a list")
        for idx, step in enumerate(self.step_results):
            _validate_step_result(step, idx)

        _validate_mapping("summary", self.summary)

    # -------------------------
    # Serialization
    # -------------------------

    def to_dict(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        return {
            "schema_version": self.schema_version,
            "execution_result_record_id": self.execution_result_record_id,
            "artifact_type": self.artifact_type,
            "authority": self.authority,
            "evidence": self.evidence,
            "determinism": self.determinism,
            "plan_record_id": self.plan_record_id,
            "decision_record_id": self.decision_record_id,
```

# PEIS — Personal Engineering Intelligence System

Based only on the PEIS project’s chat history, PEIS is a personal engineering intelligence environment designed to help one person understand, plan, execute, evaluate, and continuously improve complex technical work without surrendering authority to an AI model.

The project has progressed well beyond a loose idea. Its governing architecture is extensively defined, and a functional Python implementation already demonstrates the central planning-and-execution loop. However, the implementation currently represents the governed operational core of PEIS—not the entire broader intelligence environment envisioned by the project.

## The most accurate current definition

PEIS stands for **Personal Engineering Intelligence System**. The codename used in earlier work was **MINSTITUTION**, and the selected descriptive repository name was:

`personal-engineering-intelligence-system`

The project’s current definition is broader than some of its earlier descriptions.

Earlier chats often described PEIS primarily as a deterministic governance and execution system. On June 9, that framing was explicitly corrected: governance is an essential component of PEIS, but it is not the definition of PEIS.

The broader system is intended to augment an individual engineer’s ability to:

- Think through difficult problems.
- Learn across multiple technical domains.
- Preserve long-term project context.
- Retrieve the right information at the right time.
- Analyze evidence and competing possibilities.
- Convert intentions into structured plans.
- Validate plans before acting.
- Coordinate tools and AI systems.
- Execute bounded, authorized actions.
- Record what happened.
- Feed results back into future decisions.

The high-level intelligence cycle established in the chats is:

**Human → Memory and Continuity → Retrieval → Reasoning → Planning → Validation → Execution Support → Feedback and Learning**

This makes PEIS closer to a personal engineering operating environment than a chatbot, assistant wrapper, or isolated automation tool.

## The relationship between the broad PEIS vision and the implemented core

The project history contains two descriptions that can appear contradictory:

1. PEIS as a broad personal intelligence environment.
2. PEIS as a deterministic, governed planning-and-execution control plane.

They are best understood as two layers of the same project.

The **broad PEIS vision** is the complete environment through which the user works: continuity, retrieval, reasoning, planning, validation, execution support, and learning.

The **governed control plane** is the authoritative operational core currently being designed and implemented. It determines when an AI-generated proposal is admissible, what actions are legal, whether human approval is required, what may execute, and how the outcome is recorded.

The control plane is therefore not the whole purpose of PEIS. It is the machinery that makes the larger intelligence environment dependable.

## What PEIS does

### 1. Converts human objectives into structured engineering work

PEIS accepts a human objective that may initially be incomplete, informal, or messy. It constructs an explicit planning context and attempts to transform that objective into a structured, executable plan.

Planning is not treated as ordinary conversation. The design defines two distinct operating modes:

| Mode | Authority |
|---|---|
| **CONVERSATION** | Advisory only; cannot produce an authoritative plan or authorize execution |
| **PLANNING** | Schema-constrained, capability-bound, validated, and able to produce a `PlanRecord` |

This separation prevents normal conversational output from silently becoming executable instruction.

### 2. Uses AI models without treating them as authorities

The planned model flow is bounded:

1. A local model produces a non-authoritative draft.
2. ChatGPT may repair or adjudicate the draft if necessary.
3. A deterministic validator makes the final admissibility decision.
4. Remaining material ambiguity is escalated to the human.
5. If no valid outcome exists, the system hard-fails.

The models can propose and repair, but neither the local model nor ChatGPT can declare its own output valid or authorize its execution.

The canonical result states discussed were:

- `VALID`
- `REPAIRED_VALID`
- `ESCALATE_USER`
- `HARD_FAIL`

Recursive model debate is explicitly prohibited. PEIS uses a bounded adjudication cycle rather than allowing agents to negotiate indefinitely.

### 3. Validates plans against authoritative constraints

A proposed plan must satisfy several independent forms of legality:

- Plan and action schemas.
- Current policy bindings.
- Available capability inventory.
- Parameter admissibility rules.
- Required evidence and retrieval bindings.
- Determinism requirements.
- Human-approval requirements.
- Current stop or halt state.

An action is legal only when both the action schema and the bound capability snapshot permit it. A model cannot invent a capability merely because an action sounds reasonable.

### 4. Produces traceable, deterministic artifacts

PEIS is artifact-driven. Important decisions are represented as structured records rather than being left only in conversational text.

The canonical execution spine is:

**Request → PlanningSessionSnapshot → model draft → repair/adjudication → validation → PlanRecord → ApprovalRecord when required → ExecutionConfigRecord → execution → ExecutionResultRecord → StopArtifact on HALT**

The principal artifact types include:

- `PlanningSessionSnapshot`
- `PlanRecord`
- `ApprovalRecord`
- `ExecutionConfigRecord`
- `ExecutionResultRecord`
- `StopArtifact`
- Evidence, policy, capability, and retrieval bindings supporting those records

Authoritative artifact identity is based on canonicalized content and its bindings, including:

- Primary evidence snapshot.
- Ordered supplemental evidence snapshots.
- Policy snapshot.
- Capability inventory snapshot.
- Schema and validator versions.
- Grounding and prompt-pack versions.
- Input fingerprint.
- Relevant model context.
- Determinism envelope.

This is intended to make decisions reproducible, inspectable, and resistant to silent context changes.

### 5. Gates execution through human authorization

Where policy requires approval, validation alone is insufficient. PEIS must produce an approval request and receive an explicit approval record before execution.

Approval and execution are separate events. The system is designed so that:

- A valid plan is not automatically an authorized plan.
- Approval is recorded and bound to the plan.
- Rejection is also recorded.
- Execution uses a separately bound configuration.
- Promotion or rollback follows its own governed process.

Human authority therefore remains structurally represented instead of being an informal expectation.

### 6. Executes through registered, bounded capabilities

PEIS does not permit arbitrary model-generated shell activity. Execution is routed through a capability registry containing known action types and implementations.

The implemented action surface has included:

- `noop`
- `run_pytest`
- `identify_next_task`
- `summarize_current_blocker`
- `review_repo_state`
- `review_runtime_surface`
- `review_recent_artifacts`

These capabilities demonstrate the intended pattern, but the action surface is still narrow.

### 7. Records outcomes and stops safely

Execution produces an authoritative `ExecutionResultRecord`, including the plan binding, overall status, individual step results, summary information, and governing evidence/determinism information.

The design also defines HALT as a terminal condition:

- A `StopArtifact` must be emitted.
- Forward execution stops.
- The system cannot silently recover or resume in place.
- Recovery requires a new evaluation context.
- The human is involved when resolution cannot be determined safely.

### 8. Learns through evidence, not uncontrolled self-modification

“Feedback and learning” in PEIS does not mean the AI autonomously rewrites itself.

The intended learning loop is based on:

- Persisted plans.
- Validation failures.
- Correction cases.
- Execution results.
- Recent project artifacts.
- Human decisions.
- Future retrieval of those records as grounded examples.

This allows future planning to improve while preserving provenance and human control.

## What PEIS does not own

The project performed substantial boundary cleanup to prevent PEIS from absorbing every neighboring AI function.

PEIS is not intended to own:

- Raw ChatGPT transcript storage.
- Conversation archival.
- Embedding generation.
- Vector databases.
- Corpus ingestion.
- Retrieval indexing infrastructure.
- Long-term memory storage.
- Hardware mutation or host-level optimization.
- A user-interface chat environment as an authority.
- Hidden background retrieval.
- Implicit mode switching or implicit execution.

CICS preserves conversation continuity and structured memory. PEIS consumes that continuity through explicit interfaces. Likewise, retrieval can support PEIS, but retrieval remains non-authoritative and must be explicitly bound into a planning session.

Open WebUI was specifically classified as an interface, never the PEIS control plane.

## What has actually been implemented

The authoritative implementation was located at:

`/home/kimberly/peis`

It was also accessed from the Steam Deck through:

`/home/deck/mnt/xps_peis/`

The project uses a Python `src/` layout and a Python 3.12 virtual environment.

### Planning implementation

The implemented planning layer included components such as:

- `snapshot.py`
- `draft.py`
- `validate.py`
- `contracts.py`
- `pipeline.py`
- `escalation.py`
- `adjudicate.py`
- `recover.py`
- `ollama_adapter.py`
- `artifact_store.py`
- `retrieval.py`
- `prompt_pack.py`

Together, these provided a working flow resembling:

**PlanningRequest → PlanningSessionSnapshot → local Qwen draft → validation → escalation or ChatGPT adjudication → revalidation → validated plan**

Validated plans, failure cases, and correction cases were stored as deterministic JSON artifacts.

### Execution and persistence

The execution layer was connected to:

- A capability registry.
- Plan-driven execution.
- `ExecutionResultRecord` generation.
- Persistent planning and execution artifact stores.
- A command-line execution interface.

A verified execution of the `run_pytest` capability completed successfully and produced a stored execution record.

### Runtime gateway

A FastAPI-compatible runtime gateway existed under:

`src/peis/runtime/gateway/`

Its surfaces included:

- `/health`
- `/v1/models`
- `/v1/chat/completions`

The gateway configuration required `OPENAI_API_KEY` and supported the configured Ollama service. Startup behavior was hardened so that a missing key produced a clear readiness error rather than an obscure crash.

A separate Open WebUI experiment also established that:

- Open WebUI could run.
- Ollama and the local Qwen model could run.
- A sequential local-model-to-ChatGPT loop worked in the terminal.
- Injecting that complete flow into existing Open WebUI conversations did not work through the tested API approach.

That UI limitation does not invalidate the PEIS core because Open WebUI was subsequently placed outside the authority boundary.

### Testing and source control

The strongest verified implementation checkpoint reported:

- Core, runtime, storage, and execution integrated.
- Deterministic artifacts enforced.
- End-to-end execution-to-artifact-to-persistence verified.
- Planning completed end to end under clean host conditions.
- **149 of 149 tests passing.**
- A clean initial repository commit, `d1f43d0`, pushed to GitHub.

Later work modified artifact-driven task selection in `src/peis/execution/cli.py`. The recursion problem was fixed, although subsequent testing exposed another recommendation-quality issue.

## What remains incomplete

PEIS is not finished, and it should not yet be described as a production-ready implementation of the complete vision.

The most important remaining work is:

- Reconcile the working repository with the later canonical architecture.
- Fix remaining `PlanningSessionSnapshot` and `determinism_envelope` contract drift.
- Correct misleading normalized metadata following adjudication.
- Eliminate inappropriate promotion of generic or meta-level task recommendations.
- Expand the capability registry beyond a small set of repository-inspection and test actions.
- Improve planning reliability under host resource contention.
- Make the daily planning interface straightforward enough for normal use.
- Complete and verify approval, execution-configuration, and HALT behavior throughout the real runtime.
- Integrate explicit memory and retrieval bindings without allowing PEIS to absorb CICS or the retrieval platform.
- Turn persisted outcomes into a reliable feedback loop.
- Validate the full system across real engineering projects rather than only controlled test objectives.

A specific desired operator experience was identified as something resembling:

`peis plan "my actual problem today"`

That stable, everyday interface had not yet been completed.

## How far along the project is

PEIS is best described as being in an **advanced architecture and functional-core prototype stage**.

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| Name, mission, and broad purpose | Established |
| Boundary between PEIS and memory/retrieval systems | Established |
| Canonical governed control-plane design | Substantially complete |
| Gap-resolution and canonical synthesis | Completed; 18/18 recorded gaps resolved |
| Planning pipeline | Implemented and demonstrated |
| Validation and bounded model adjudication | Implemented in first-pass form |
| Deterministic plan/result persistence | Implemented |
| Execution capability framework | Implemented but narrow |
| FastAPI runtime gateway | Implemented |
| Automated tests | 149/149 passing at strongest verified checkpoint |
| Human-approval lifecycle | Canonically specified; full runtime completion not established |
| Execution configuration and EEO | Specified; full implementation not established |
| HALT/StopArtifact lifecycle | Specified; full end-to-end implementation not established |
| Memory, continuity, and retrieval integration | Boundaries established; broader integration incomplete |
| Feedback and learning loop | Partially supported through artifacts; not complete |
| Stable daily-use operator experience | Incomplete |
| Complete Personal Engineering Intelligence System | Not yet implemented |

The April reconstruction work marked **Phase 4 — Canonical PEIS Synthesis** complete and described the project as ready for **Phase 5 rebuild preparation**. That should not be interpreted as starting from nothing. A working repository already exists. “Rebuild” means bringing that implementation into full alignment with the cleaned, canonical design.

In practical terms, PEIS already has a functioning vertical slice:

**objective → grounded planning → AI draft → validation/adjudication → validated plan → registered execution → deterministic result artifact → persistence**

What it does not yet have is the breadth, integration, reliability, and operator experience necessary to make that loop the complete personal engineering intelligence environment originally envisioned.

# Personal Engineering Intelligence System (PEIS)

## Mission

Personal Engineering Intelligence System (PEIS) is an operational intelligence framework for transforming intentions into outcomes.

It exists to help individuals and teams plan, execute, evaluate, and continuously improve complex work while preserving context, decisions, accountability, and continuity across time.

PEIS explores how human and AI collaboration can be structured to support reliable execution without sacrificing transparency, governance, or human oversight.

---

## Why PEIS Exists

Ideas are abundant.

Execution is difficult.

Most projects do not fail because of a lack of intelligence, creativity, or opportunity. They fail because plans drift, priorities change, decisions are forgotten, lessons are lost, and continuity breaks.

People begin with clear intentions.

Over time:

* Goals become fragmented
* Context disappears
* Decisions lose traceability
* Execution becomes inconsistent
* Progress becomes difficult to evaluate
* Knowledge becomes disconnected from action

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into professional and personal workflows, these challenges become more significant.

PEIS exists to provide operational continuity between intention, execution, evaluation, and improvement.

---

## Core Question

PEIS exists to explore a fundamental question:

> How can complex work remain coordinated, accountable, and effective as people, projects, systems, and AI capabilities evolve over time?

---

## Operational Lifecycle

PEIS views execution as a continuous cycle:

```text
Intent
  ↓
Plan
  ↓
Execution
  ↓
Outcome
  ↓
Evaluation
  ↓
Improvement
```

Every stage produces information that can be reviewed, preserved, and used to improve future outcomes.

---

## Core Functions

### Planning

Transform goals, observations, and requirements into structured plans that can be executed and evaluated.

### Execution

Coordinate actions across people, systems, tools, and workflows.

### Evaluation

Measure outcomes against expectations and identify gaps between intended and actual results.

### Decision Preservation

Maintain records of important decisions, assumptions, tradeoffs, and rationale.

### Operational Continuity

Preserve project state across conversations, repositories, systems, and time.

### Continuous Improvement

Convert experience, successes, failures, and observations into future capability.

---

## Core Principles

### Intent Before Action

Execution should be guided by clearly understood objectives.

### Decisions Should Be Traceable

Actions should remain connected to the reasoning that produced them.

### Continuity Matters

Short-term efficiency should not come at the expense of long-term understanding.

### Human Oversight

Humans remain responsible for priorities, legitimacy, accountability, and final authority.

### Continuous Learning

Every project should improve the ability to execute future projects.

---

## Relationship to blAIne

PEIS is a foundational component of the broader blAIne ecosystem.

```text
blAIne
│
├── The Human Capability Project (THCP)
│   └── Human capability, agency, and governance
│
├── Knowledge Governance Infrastructure (KGI)
│   └── Knowledge preservation, governance, and continuity
│
├── Personal Engineering Intelligence System (PEIS)
│   └── Planning, execution, evaluation, and operational continuity
│
└── Future infrastructure initiatives
```

Within the ecosystem, PEIS serves as the operational layer responsible for transforming goals, knowledge, and decisions into coordinated action.

---

## Areas of Development

Current areas of work include:

* Planning systems
* Execution workflows
* Evaluation frameworks
* Decision tracking
* Operational continuity
* Human-AI collaboration
* Project governance
* Workflow orchestration
* Capability development systems

---

## Long-Term Vision

The long-term vision of PEIS is to support durable operational systems capable of helping individuals and organizations execute complex work with greater clarity, continuity, accountability, and effectiveness.

The objective is not simply to manage tasks.

The objective is to create systems that help intentions become outcomes, outcomes become learning, and learning become future capability.

PEIS is an exploration of how disciplined execution can remain effective in an increasingly AI-augmented world.

            "This chat actually produced quite a few.\n\nWhat's interesting is that they are less about AI and more about **epistemology, governance, reality, and reproducibility**.\n\nThese are the ones that jumped out at me.\n\n---\n\n# Identity / Reality\n\n### Nugget 1\n\n> Identity defines what exists. Decision defines what changes.\n\nThis is probably the strongest single statement in the entire design.\n\n---\n\n### Nugget 2\n\n> Nothing else defines reality.\n\nThe follow-up is what makes the first statement powerful.\n\n---\n\n### Nugget 3\n\n> Retrieval can support identity. Retrieval can never define identity.\n\nThis is essentially the lesson learned from every RAG hallucination problem.\n\n---\n\n### Nugget 4\n\n> Structure must define existence before retrieval can describe it.\n\nA more approachable version of the same idea.\n\n---\n\n# Validation / Truth\n\n### Nugget 5\n\n> Validation is not a feeling. Reality still needs an anchor.\n\n---\n\n# Authority\n\n### Nugget 13\n\n> Authority determines allowed sources.\n\nThis is one of those deceptively simple statements.\n\n---\n\n### Nugget 14\n\n> Not all information is equally qualified to answer all questions.\n\nA public-friendly translation.\n\n---\n\n### Nugget 15\n\n> The answer to a question depends on what sources are permitted to define it.\n\nVery strong.\n\n---\n\n# Ambiguity\n\n### Nugget 16\n\n> Ambiguity ignored becomes error.\n\nShort and good.\n\n---\n\n### Nugget 17\n\n> No silent guessing.\n\nOne of the core doctrines.\n\n---\n\n### Nugget 18\n\n> If confidence is insufficient, escalation is required.\n\nThis applies far beyond AI.\n\n---\n\n# Determinism\n\n### Nugget 19\n\n> Same inputs.             "Locked. Based on that, the environment design is now pin-able.\n\n## PEIS Planning Environment v1\n\n### 1. Authority and role split\n\nThis environment has four layers with strict authority boundaries:\n\n**PEIS**\nAuthoritative execution system. Sole authority for schemas, capability legality, validation outcome, execution, and persisted artifacts.\n\n**qwen2.5:3b**\nGrounded draft generator only. Produces a structured candidate plan draft inside a constrained action surface. Never trusted directly.\n\n**Deterministic validator/rewriter**\nStructural gate. Enforces schema, allowed actions, required fields, and repair rules. This is the first hard boundary between model output and PEIS.\n\n**ChatGPT**\nSecond-pass adjudicating planner. Invoked only when deterministic repair cannot produce a valid plan or when ambiguity/failure/halt conditions are detected.\n\nThat preserves your stated architecture:\nqwen drafts, validator gates, ChatGPT adjudicates, PEIS remains authority.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Session snapshot contract\n\nEach planning session should begin by materializing a **PlanningSessionSnapshot**. This is the deterministic planning envelope.\n\nIt should bind:\n\n- `capability_inventory_snapshot_id`\n- `policy_snapshot_id`\n- `grounding_corpus_version`\n- `model_id`\n- `model_hash` if available\n- `prompt_pack_version`\n- `plan_schema_version`\n- `action_schema_version`\n- `curated_examples_set_id`\n- optional `relevant_execution_examples_set_id`\n\nThis snapshot is loaded once at startup and held fixed for the session.\n\n### Required invariant\nNo plan generation should occur without an explicit session snapshot.  \nEvery emitted candidate plan and validated plan should reference that snapshot or its component IDs.\n\nThis gives you a deterministic planning substrate even if raw model tokens vary.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Grounding stack precedence\n\nYou already locked the precedence. The implementation should reflect it literally.\n\n### Layer 1 — schema-constrained generation layer\nThis dominates everything else.\n\nThis layer provides:\n\n- the only allowed top-level fields\n- the only allowed action types\n- allowed step shapes\n- required/optional field rules\n- step ordering constraints if any\n- enum restrictions\n- forbidden fields\n- canonical serialization expectations\n\nThis should be injected as a **machine-readable action surface**, not prose only.\n\n### Layer 2 — strict prompt pack / role contract\nThis tells qwen what it is doing and what it is not allowed to do.\n\nThe prompt pack should define:\n\n- qwen is a PEIS draft planner\n- qwen may only use capabilities present in the current snapshot\n- qwen must not invent domains, capabilities, or fields\n- qwen must output only structured draft content\n- qwen must prefer omission over invention\n- qwen must explicitly mark unresolved ambiguity rather than hallucinate\n\n### Layer 3 — retrieval context\nThis should be narrow and curated.\n\nAllowed retrieval sources:\n\n- capability inventory snapshot\n- current policy snapshot summary\n- plan schema summary\n- curated valid PlanRecord examples\n- relevant successful prior plans only when explicitly relevant\n- curated failure/correction examples\n\nDo **not** dump broad execution history into context.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Persistent environment structure\n\nYou need a durable planning substrate. The simplest clean form is a dedicated environment directory.\n\nExample:\n\n```text\npeis_planning_env/\n├── snapshots/\n│   ├── capability_inventory/\n│   ├── policy/\n│   ├── grounding/\n│   ├── prompt_packs/\n│   └── session/\n├── corpus/\n│   ├── canonical/\n│   │   ├── schemas/\n│   │   ├── capability_inventory/\n│   │   ├── policy/\n│   │   └── prompt_pack/\n│   ├── examples/\n│   │   ├── valid_plans/\n│   │   ├── failure_cases/\n│   │   └── correction_cases/\n│   └── retrieval_index/\n├── runtime/\n│   ├── requests/\n│   ├── drafts/\n│   ├── repaired/\n│   ├── escalations/\n│   └── validated/\n└── logs/\n```\n\n### What persists across sessions\n\nPersist exactly what you locked:\n\n- capability inventory snapshots\n- prompt pack / role contract versions\n- grounding corpus versions\n- prior validated plans\n- failure cases and correction examples\n\n### Important rule\nPersisted failure/correction examples are **instructional**, not authoritative.  \nSchemas, policy, and capability inventory remain authoritative.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Planning pipeline\n\nThis is the concrete flow.\n\n### Phase A — startup binding\nAt startup:\n\n1. load current capability inventory\n2. load current policy snapshot\n3. load current prompt pack version\n4. load current schema versions\n5. build or load grounding corpus version\n6. produce `PlanningSessionSnapshot`\n7. expose only that bound snapshot to the session\n\nNo planning should happen before this completes.\n\n---\n\n### Phase B — request normalization\nUser asks for work. The environment normalizes that request into a stable internal planning input.\n\nExample internal object:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"planning_request_id\": \"…\",\n  \"objective\": \"Run the PEIS test suite\",\n  \"constraints\": [\n    \"use known capabilities only\",\n    \"emit PEIS-valid structured draft only\"\n  ],\n  \"session_snapshot_id\": \"…\"\n}\n```\n\nThis isolates raw conversational phrasing from planning input.\n\n---\n\n### Phase C — qwen draft generation\nqwen receives only:\n\n- role contract\n- allowed output shape\n- capability inventory snapshot\n- policy snapshot summary\n- minimal relevant examples\n- the normalized planning request\n\nqwen should output a **candidate structured draft**, not a freeform answer.\n\nFor example, the output surface should be restricted toward something like:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"objective\": \"…\",\n  \"steps\": [\n    {\n      \"step_id\": \"01\",\n      \"action_type\": \"run_pytest\",\n      \"description\": \"Run pytest with minimal verbosity\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nThe exact shape should mirror your locked PEIS planning surface.\n\n---\n\n### Phase D — deterministic validation and repair\nThis is the most important operational layer.\n\nThe validator/rewriter should apply fixed repair passes in ordered sequence.\n\n#### Repair pass classes\n1. **structure normalization**\n   - missing top-level containers\n   - field ordering\n   - canonical key names\n   - trimming commentary outside JSON\n\n2. **schema repair**\n   - remove forbidden fields\n   - coerce simple type mismatches if allowed\n   - fill deterministic defaults if policy permits\n\n3. **capability legality repair**\n   - reject unknown `action_type`\n   - reject capability aliases\n   - reject domain inventions\n   - reject actions not present in current capability snapshot\n\n4. **plan hygiene repair**\n   - renumber step IDs if deterministic rules allow\n   - remove duplicate no-op garbage\n   - reject semantically empty steps\n\n5. **policy gate**\n   - reject disallowed actions\n   - reject unsafe or policy-conflicting plans\n\n### Result categories\nThe validator must emit one of:\n\n- `VALID`\n- `REPAIRED_VALID`\n- `ESCALATE_CHATGPT`\n- `HARD_FAIL`\n\nNo silent freeform fallback.\n\n---\n\n## 6. ChatGPT escalation contract\n\nChatGPT should not be in the hot path unless needed.\n\n### Escalate only when:\n- deterministic repair failed\n- ambiguity blocks safe plan formation\n- capability misuse indicates semantic confusion\n- the request implicates a halt or governance-sensitive condition\n- multiple valid interpretations exist and deterministic repair cannot choose\n\n### ChatGPT input bundle\nWhen escalation occurs, send:\n\n- original normalized request\n- qwen draft\n- validator failure report\n- capability inventory snapshot\n- policy snapshot summary\n- prompt pack version\n- minimal relevant examples\n\n### ChatGPT task\nNot “please plan from scratch” by default. Instead:\n\n- diagnose why draft failed\n- repair into PEIS-valid candidate plan\n- preserve user intent\n- use only available capabilities\n- return only compliant plan payload\n\nIf ChatGPT still cannot produce a valid plan, hard-fail.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Capability inventory handling\n\nBecause you locked startup refresh, the environment should treat capability discovery as a startup-time build artifact.\n\n### Startup behavior\nOn startup:\n\n- enumerate registered capabilities\n- build canonical manifest\n- assign snapshot ID\n- expose only that manifest for the full session\n\n### Session behavior\nDuring the session:\n\n- do not mutate visible capability surface\n- do not re-query registry for each prompt\n- if the runtime detects inventory drift, mark session stale and require new startup snapshot\n\nThis prevents cross-session drift and mid-session inconsistency.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Prompt pack design\n\nYou need a versioned prompt pack, not ad hoc instructions.\n\nSuggested pack structure:\n\n```text\nprompt_pack_v1/\n├── system_role.txt\n├── capability_usage_rules.txt\n├── domain_invention_prohibition.txt\n├── output_contract.txt\n├── ambiguity_policy.txt\n└── examples_manifest.json\n```\n\n### System role content should include:\n- you are a PEIS draft planner\n- you may only use actions from current capability inventory\n- do not invent actions, fields, or execution domains\n- output only structured candidate plan\n- if uncertain, express uncertainty within allowed schema or omit unsupported steps\n- never explain outside the payload unless specifically requested by the environment\n\n### Critical point\nThe prompt pack should not be the only defense.             "Good. That verifies the real loop.\n\nWhat is now true:\n\n- local draft generation can fail\n- failure is validated against the real execution capability surface\n- illegal action types are blocked before execution\n- escalation payload is built correctly\n- adjudicated repair is revalidated against the same legality surface\n- only a PEIS-legal repaired plan survives\n\nThat is the first version that matches the actual requirement closely enough to keep.\n\nCurrent planning files:\n- `snapshot.py`\n- `schemas/PlanningSessionSnapshotSchema_1.json`\n- `draft.py`\n- `validate.py`\n- `pipeline.py`\n- `escalation.py`\n- `adjudicate.py`\n- `recover.py`\n- `contracts.py`\n\nThe remaining weak point is the model adapter:\n- right now the real path still depends on subprocess + `ollama run`\n- that is not the reusable persistent adapter you want\n\nThe next correct step is to replace the ad hoc CLI invocation with a real Ollama HTTP adapter, so planning talks to the XPS-hosted Ollama service directly and cleanly.\n\nCreate:\n\n`src/peis/planning/ollama_adapter.py`\n\nUse this full file:\n\n```python\nimport json\nfrom typing import Any, Dict, Optional\nfrom urllib import request, error\n\n\ndef invoke_ollama_generate(\n    *,\n    prompt: str,\n    model: str,\n    base_url: str = \"http://127.0.0.1:11434\",\n    options: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,\n) -> str:\n    \"\"\"\n    Invoke Ollama's /api/generate endpoint and return the final response text.\n\n    This adapter is deterministic at the transport layer. Model-level determinism\n    still depends on the options and model behavior you choose to supply.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    payload: Dict[str, Any] = {\n        \"model\": model,\n        \"prompt\": prompt,\n        \"stream\": False,\n    }\n\n    if options is not None:\n        payload[\"options\"] = options\n\n    body = json.dumps(payload).encode(\"utf-8\")\n\n    req = request.Request(\n        url=f\"{base_url.rstrip('/')}/api/generate\",\n        data=body,\n        headers={\"Content-Type\": \"application/json\"},\n        method=\"POST\",\n    )\n\n    try:\n        with request.urlopen(req) as resp:\n            response_body = resp.read().decode(\"utf-8\")\n    except error.HTTPError as exc:\n        detail = exc.read().decode(\"utf-8\", errors=\"replace\")\n        raise RuntimeError(f\"ollama HTTP error {exc.code}: {detail}\") from exc\n    except error.URLError as exc:\n        raise RuntimeError(f\"ollama connection error: {exc}\") from exc\n\n    try:\n        parsed = json.loads(response_body)\n    except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:\n        raise RuntimeError(f\"invalid JSON from ollama: {exc}\") from exc\n\n    response_text = parsed.get(\"response\")\n    if not isinstance(response_text, str):\n        raise RuntimeError(\"ollama response missing string field: response\")\n\n    return response_text\n```\n\nThen verify on the XPS:\n\n```bash\ncd ~/peis && PYTHONPATH=src python - <<'PY'\nfrom peis.planning.ollama_adapter import invoke_ollama_generate\n\nresult = invoke_ollama_generate(\n    prompt='Reply with exactly: {\"ok\":true}',\n    model=\"qwen2.5:3b\",\n)\n\nprint(result)\nPY\n```\n\nExpected:\n- non-empty output\n- probably still not exact, but it should return model text through HTTP cleanly\n\nAfter that, the next step is one targeted replacement to use this adapter in the recovery test path instead of subprocess."

## Assistant

The point of this chat, based on the hand-off, is to design the layer that comes **after governance review is complete**.

Up to this point, KGI has primarily proven:

1. Raw chats can be preserved.
2. Information can be extracted.
3. Human review can validate or reject extraction.
4. Information can be routed.
5. Governance findings can be audited.

What has *not* been designed yet is what happens **after routing**.

The hand-off explicitly identifies the realization that emerged during the audit:

> The user's actual objective is not governance findings.

Governance findings are merely a safety mechanism.

The actual objective is:

- project continuity
- knowledge recovery
- ecosystem discovery
- overlap detection
- forgotten project recovery
- project identity preservation
- cross-project contamination prevention

So the purpose of this chat is to answer:

> Once a reviewed fact has been routed somewhere, how does KGI turn that routed evidence into usable continuity intelligence?

Or more concretely:

Current KGI:

```text
Raw Chat
    ↓
Extraction
    ↓
Review
    ↓
Routing
```

Missing KGI:

```text
Routing
    ↓
Project Knowledge
    ↓
Continuity Intelligence
    ↓
Overlap Detection
    ↓
Ecosystem Discovery
```

The questions this chat is supposed to answer are things like:

### Project Knowledge

How does a project accumulate knowledge over time?

Example:

```text
TranslAItor
    CHAT-000032
    CHAT-000109
    CHAT-000284
    CHAT-000711
```

What artifact actually represents the current state of knowledge for TranslAItor?

---

### Continuity Intelligence

How do we detect:

```text
You talked about this six months ago.
```

or

```text
This project already solved this problem.
```

or

```text
This decision contradicts a previous decision.
```

---

### Rename Detection

Example:

```text
Project A
```

later becomes

```text
Project B
```

without anyone realizing they are the same thing.

How does KGI surface:

```text
Possible project rename.
Human review required.
```

without automatically merging them?

---

### Duplicate Project Detection

Example:

```text
System X
```

and

```text
System Y
```

both claim to:

```text
Perform evidence routing.
```

How does KGI detect the overlap and surface it for review?

---

### Shared Subsystem Discovery

This is the realization you described during the audit.

Example:

```text
Project A uses identity management.

Project B uses identity management.

Project C uses identity management.
```

KGI should eventually be able to say:

```text
Recurring capability detected.

Potential shared subsystem candidate.

Review required.
```

without deciding that it actually *is* a subsystem.

---

### Ecosystem Discovery

Eventually KGI should be able to produce something like:

```text
TranslAItor
    └─ depends on Trust Framework

NarrAIator
    └─ depends on Identity Framework

PEIS
    └─ depends on Capability Registry

AI Diagnostician
    └─ depends on Capability Registry
```

and reveal ecosystem structure that emerged from evidence.

Not because someone manually drew it.

Because the evidence repeatedly pointed to it.

---

So, in one sentence:

**The point of this chat is to design the layer that converts validated routed evidence into project memory, continuity intelligence, overlap detection, and ecosystem discovery while preserving human authority and evidence traceability.**

That is the major layer that currently does not exist in KGI.

## User

agreed. where do we start, and what is the plan to accomplish this?

## Assistant

I think the first thing we need to do is identify the **minimum artifact architecture** required to support the objective.

Right now KGI already has:

```text
Raw Chat
    ↓
Extraction Report
    ↓
Review Record
    ↓
Routing Packet
```

The temptation is to immediately start designing overlap detection, ecosystem maps, rename detection, and project intelligence.

I do not think that is the correct first step.

None of those things can exist until we answer a more fundamental question:

> Where does project knowledge actually live?

At the moment, routing packets can say:

```text
Route Item X → TranslAItor
Route Item Y → PEIS
Route Item Z → AI Diagnostician
```

But after routing occurs there is no authoritative project-level artifact that accumulates the routed knowledge.

Without that, there is nothing to compare.

Nothing to analyze.

Nothing to detect overlap against.

Nothing to build continuity from.

---

## Phase 1 — Project Knowledge Architecture

Design:

```text
Project Knowledge Record (PKR)
```

Questions:

- What is a project?
- How is project identity represented?
- What evidence can be attached?
- What does a project know?
- What does it not know?
- How are unknowns preserved?
- How are sources traced?

Goal:

Create the first artifact that can accumulate routed evidence over time.

Without PKR, everything else is impossible.

---

## Phase 2 — Continuity Architecture

Once project knowledge exists:

Design:

```text
Continuity Record (CR)
```

Purpose:

Capture continuity-relevant observations.

Examples:

```text
Prior decision referenced.

Prior capability referenced.

Potential contradiction detected.

Potential duplicate effort detected.

Potential forgotten project detected.
```

Important:

These are observations.

Not conclusions.

---

## Phase 3 — Relationship Architecture

Only after projects have knowledge and continuity records.

Design:

```text
Relationship Record (RR)
```

Examples:

```text
Project A references Project B.

Project A shares capability with Project C.

Project A depends on capability from Project D.
```

Still:

No automatic merging.

No authority.

Only evidence-backed relationships.

---

## Phase 4 — Overlap Architecture

Now KGI has enough evidence to compare.

Design:

```text
Overlap Record (OR)
```

Examples:

```text
Potential duplicate capability.

Potential duplicate project.

Potential project rename.

Potential subsystem overlap.
```

These become review artifacts.

Not automatic actions.

---

## Phase 5 — Ecosystem Architecture

Only now can ecosystem discovery happen.

Design:

```text
Ecosystem Record (ER)
```

Purpose:

Represent reviewed ecosystem structure.

Examples:

```text
Shared subsystem candidates.

Capability clusters.

Project families.

Dependency networks.
```

Again:

Discovery is descriptive.

Not authoritative.

---

## Phase 6 — Human Review Architecture

Every phase above requires review gates.

Design:

```text
Project Review
Continuity Review
Relationship Review
Overlap Review
Ecosystem Review
```

Otherwise KGI eventually becomes an inference engine pretending to be governance.

The hand-off explicitly identifies that as a drift risk.

---

## The Immediate Next Step

I would not start with overlap.

I would not start with ecosystem maps.

I would not start with rename detection.

I would start with a single question:

> What is the authoritative artifact that represents a project's accumulated knowledge after routing?

Because every other capability depends on that answer.

So the next concrete design task is:

```text
Project Knowledge Record (PKR)

Purpose
Authority
Contents
Evidence model
Source traceability
Update workflow
Review workflow
Unknown handling
Relationship to routing packets
```

That is the foundation layer for everything the hand-off describes. Without it, continuity intelligence has nowhere to live.

# Step 18 — Minimum Viable System (MVS)

## Objective

Design the smallest possible implementation capable of processing **one real chat** through the complete governance lifecycle:

```text
RECEIVED
↓
REGISTERED
↓
EXTRACTED
↓
REVIEWED
↓
ROUTED
↓
ARCHIVED
```

while preserving all currently locked governance decisions.

---

# MVS Design Principles

The MVS exists to validate governance, not automation.

The goal is **not**:

- bulk ingestion
- automation
- scalability
- ecosystem discovery at scale

The goal is:

> Can one chat be processed correctly under governance rules?

If yes:

- schemas can be tested
- SOP can be tested
- audit trail can be tested
- overlap handling can be tested
- human review can be tested

---

# MVS Scope Boundary

Included:

- One chat
- Manual review
- Local storage
- JSON artifacts
- Audit trail

Excluded:

- Batch processing
- Search engine
- Embeddings
- LLM automation
- Database
- UI
- Web application
- Multi-user support

---

# Minimum Repository Structure

```text
chat_sorter/

├── chats/
│   └── incoming/
│
├── artifacts/
│   ├── extraction_reports/
│   ├── routing_packets/
│   └── canonical_artifacts/
│
├── reviews/
│
├── archive/
│
├── manifests/
│
├── schemas/
│
├── scripts/
│
└── README.md
```

Nothing else is required for MVS.

---

# Required Schemas

Only schemas required to process one chat.

```text
schemas/

chat_manifest.schema.json

extraction_report.schema.json

routing_packet.schema.json

canonical_artifact.schema.json
```

All other schemas remain conceptual until needed.

---

# Required Scripts

Only four scripts.

## 1. register_chat.py

Purpose:

```text
Incoming Chat
↓
Assign Chat ID
↓
Create Manifest Entry
```

Produces:

```text
chat_manifest.json
```

---

## 2. create_extraction.py

Purpose:

Create initial extraction report.

Produces:

```text
extraction_report.json
```

Initially this can be human-generated and merely validated.

---

## 3. validate_artifact.py

Purpose:

Validate any artifact against schema.

Used on:

- manifest
- extraction report
- routing packet
- canonical artifact

---

## 4. archive_chat.py

Purpose:

Move completed chat package into archive state.

Creates immutable archive record.

---

# First Chat Processing Workflow

## Stage 1 — Receive

Human selects one chat.

Example:

```text
ChatGPT Recents

Website Revision Strategy
```

Raw chat exported.

Stored:

```text
chats/incoming/
```

Raw chat is immutable evidence.

---

## Stage 2 — Register

Run:

```bash
python register_chat.py
```

Produces:

```json
{
  "chat_id": "CHAT-000001",
  "status": "REGISTERED"
}
```

Manifest updated.

---

## Stage 3 — Extract

Human performs extraction.

Produces:

```json
{
  "chat_id": "CHAT-000001",
  "candidate_projects": [],
  "candidate_artifacts": [],
  "candidate_concepts": [],
  "candidate_overlaps": []
}
```

Stored:

```text
artifacts/extraction_reports/
```

No routing yet.

No interpretation yet.

Only extraction.

---

## Stage 4 — Review

Human reviews extraction.

Possible outcomes:

```text
APPROVED
REJECTED
NEEDS_REVISION
UNKNOWN
```

Stored:

```text
reviews/
```

This is the first authoritative decision point.

---

## Stage 5 — Route

After approval:

Routing packet created.

Example:

```json
{
  "artifact_id": "ART-000001",
  "routing_destination": "TranslAItor",
  "routing_reason": "Evidence supports relevance"
}
```

Important:

Routing destination is not ownership.

Locked governance remains intact.

---

## Stage 6 — Archive

Run:

```bash
python archive_chat.py
```

Archive package contains:

```text
raw_chat
manifest
extraction_report
review_record
routing_packet
```

Stored:

```text
archive/
```

Chat becomes immutable historical evidence.

---

# Minimum Review Record

New artifact required.

```text
reviews/review_record.json
```

Contains:

```json
{
  "review_id": "REV-000001",
  "chat_id": "CHAT-000001",
  "review_status": "APPROVED",
  "reviewer": "human",
  "timestamp": "..."
}
```

This is necessary because human review authority is locked governance.

Without it:

Review authority cannot be audited.

---

# Minimum Manifest Contents

Manifest only needs:

```json
{
  "chat_id": "CHAT-000001",
  "source_location": "ChatGPT Recents",
  "received_timestamp": "...",
  "lifecycle_state": "REGISTERED"
}
```

Nothing more is required.

---

# Success Criteria

The MVS succeeds if one chat can produce:

```text
Raw Chat
✓

Manifest
✓

Extraction Report
✓

Review Record
✓

Routing Packet
✓

Archive Record
✓
```

and every artifact can be validated against schema.

---

# MVS Deliverable

At completion, the repository should be capable of answering:

> "Show me every decision made about this chat and the evidence supporting it."

using only:

```text
raw_chat
manifest
extraction_report
review_record
routing_packet
archive_record
```

If that question can be answered completely, the governance model has survived first contact with reality.

That constitutes a valid Step 18 MVS under all currently locked project constraints.

## User

I'd like to discuss an issue I see, and I want to talk about a work around. I'm not sure where OpenAI gets the audacity to try to limit how many characters I can highlight and copy in my fucking web browser on my fucking computer, but it's absolutely bull shit and I need to find a workaround so that I can copy whatever the fuck I want out of an existing chat, without the amount of characters I can actually copy being limited.

## Assistant

Yes. There are several ways around the selection/copy behavior without relying on ChatGPT’s normal highlight mechanics. I’ll separate the methods that recover a whole conversation from the quick browser-console method for extracting what is currently loaded.

## Assistant

fast|site:help.openai.com ChatGPT export data conversations chat.html export data|30|help.openai.com
fast|site:help.openai.com ChatGPT copy conversation export chat history browser|30|help.openai.com
length|short

## Assistant

Yes. You should be able to extract the text from a conversation without depending on click-and-drag selection in the ChatGPT UI.

I also would not assume the behavior you’re seeing is necessarily an intentional “you may only copy X characters” policy. Very long ChatGPT conversations use a fairly complicated frontend, and rendering/virtualization can interfere with browser selection. Either way, the practical result is the same: **the UI should not be the only way you can retrieve your own conversation text.**

### Fast workaround in Chrome

For an existing conversation, open the conversation, press **F12**, select **Console**, and run this:

```javascript
(() => {
  const messages = [...document.querySelectorAll('[data-message-author-role]')];

  const text = messages.map((el, i) => {
    const role = el.getAttribute('data-message-author-role') || 'unknown';

    return [
      `===== MESSAGE ${i + 1} — ${role.toUpperCase()} =====`,
      el.innerText.trim()
    ].join('\n');
  }).join('\n\n');

  copy(text);

  console.log(
    `Copied ${text.length.toLocaleString()} characters from ${messages.length} messages.`
  );
})();
```

That does **not highlight anything**. It reads the conversation text directly from the page DOM and puts it on your clipboard.

So if Chrome's visual selection craps out at, say, 100,000 characters, that limitation is irrelevant to this method.

There is one important caveat: **very long conversations may be virtualized**. In that case, ChatGPT may remove older messages from the DOM while you're looking at newer ones. If the console reports something suspicious like:

> Copied 84,321 characters from 17 messages

when you know the conversation contains 200 messages, then we've hit virtualization rather than a clipboard limit.

### For enormous chats, I would build around virtualization

We can make a slightly more sophisticated Chrome script that:

1. finds the ChatGPT conversation's scroll container;
2. starts at the top;
3. walks downward through the entire conversation;
4. captures each user/assistant message as ChatGPT renders it;
5. deduplicates messages that appear during overlapping scroll positions;
6. reconstructs the whole conversation;
7. copies it to the clipboard **or downloads it as Markdown/text/JSON**.

That would effectively give you a **"Rip this entire ChatGPT conversation out of the webpage"** function.

And unlike the normal selection mechanism, there would be no meaningful character limit other than browser memory.

### There is also an official bulk-recovery path

OpenAI currently provides **Settings → Data controls → Export data**. The resulting ZIP includes your chat history. OpenAI says exports can take up to seven days, so that's useful as an archival/backstop mechanism, but not as a practical tool when you're sitting in a chat and need its contents right now. citeturn888753search3turn888753search6

For what you're doing with preserving old project conversations and recovering project context, I think the better solution is actually the browser extractor rather than depending on export. It could output something like:

```text
ChatGPT Conversation
Title: Movie Library Cataloging
Conversation ID: ...
Captured: 2026-08-25

## User
...

## Assistant
...

## User
...

## Assistant
...
```

or structured JSON:

```json
{
  "title": "...",
  "conversation_id": "...",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "text": "..."
    },
    {
      "role": "assistant",
      "text": "..."
    }
  ]
}
```

That could eventually plug directly into your project-context recovery process rather than you manually highlighting half-million-character conversations. memcite

## User

## Assistant

## Assistant

Yes. What you are describing is real, and I found the mechanism behind it.

It is **not primarily Chrome running out of clipboard memory**. ChatGPT's web interface is **virtualizing/windowing long conversations**. In a sufficiently long thread, only a small portion of the conversation exists in the browser's DOM at any one time. As you scroll, older messages are actually **removed from the DOM** and different messages are mounted in their place. A recent OpenAI community report describes exactly this behavior, and OpenAI Support acknowledged the underlying long-conversation problem. citeturn725644search8turn725644search11

That explains both things you're seeing:

- **Ctrl+A → Ctrl+C:** it cannot copy messages that aren't currently instantiated in the webpage.
- **Start highlighting at the top and drag all the way down:** while you travel downward, the frontend can unmount portions you already passed. Your selection therefore cannot remain attached to one giant continuous body of text.

So yes: **from your perspective, ChatGPT is preventing the browser from copying the whole damn chat.** The important correction is only *how* it is happening. It isn't necessarily a fixed `100,000-character clipboard limit`; the page is refusing to keep the whole conversation resident in the DOM simultaneously.

Interestingly, OpenAI's current release notes specifically advertise improved `Ctrl+A` behavior intended to select conversation content, but long-thread virtualization can still defeat that because unmounted content isn't available to browser selection in the first place. citeturn725644search7turn725644search11

### The workaround I think we should use

**Stop using browser text selection entirely.**

There are already working tools using two approaches that prove this is feasible.

One current Chrome extension, **ChatGPT Thread Exporter**, explicitly says it was designed for ChatGPT's dynamically mounted conversations introduced in 2026 and **reads the conversation data model rather than relying on Ctrl+A**. citeturn725644search10

Another current script handles virtualization by automatically scrolling through the entire conversation, capturing each message while it becomes mounted, deduplicating messages by ID, and ultimately producing a Markdown file. It was tested against the 2026 ChatGPT interface. citeturn725644search15

There's also a more comprehensive open-source exporter that retrieves conversations through the authenticated browser session and produces both raw JSON and Markdown. citeturn725644search6

For **your use case**, I would not make clipboard copy the primary output at all.

I'd build a small local Chrome userscript/extension that gives you something like:

```text
Export Chat
```

When pressed:

```text
Conversation detected
↓
walk entire conversation
↓
capture every user message
capture every assistant message
capture code blocks
capture links
capture timestamps/IDs where available
↓
verify message count
↓
SAVE
```

And produce:

```text
Movie_Library_Cataloging_2026-08-25.md
Movie_Library_Cataloging_2026-08-25.json
```

Then optionally:

```text
COPY ALL
```

from **our reconstructed copy**, not ChatGPT's DOM.

That distinction matters. Once we've reconstructed the conversation ourselves, OpenAI's frontend virtualization is irrelevant.

### Even better for what you're doing

Because you're recovering enormous old project chats, I think we should make this a proper local tool rather than some disposable console snippet.

It could have:

```text
[ Export Current Chat ]
[ Copy Entire Chat ]
[ Save Markdown ]
[ Save Raw JSON ]

Messages found:       347
User messages:        174
Assistant messages:   173
Characters:           1,847,392

Capture status: COMPLETE
```

And I would make **the file the authoritative artifact**, not the clipboard.

Then a 2-million-character conversation, 5-million-character conversation, whatever, isn't dependent upon:

- DOM virtualization
- text-selection behavior
- Ctrl+A
- clipboard UI
- dragging for twenty fucking minutes
- whether ChatGPT decides to unmount the top half while you're selecting the bottom half

The official OpenAI export remains a fallback and does include chat history, but it can take **up to seven days**, so it is completely inappropriate for "I need this conversation right now." citeturn725644search2

So I think we have identified the right problem now: **we need to bypass ChatGPT's rendered conversation layer altogether, not figure out how to make Chrome select more text.**

And given the amount of old project context you're trying to recover, I think building our own **local ChatGPT Conversation Extractor** is worth doing rather than trusting a third-party extension. memcite

The **best method is not to record the highlight**. We can do that, but it still leaves OpenAI's virtualized DOM in control of what exists at any instant.

I would build the extractor so that **the moment any part of the conversation becomes available to the browser, we permanently cache it locally**. After that, ChatGPT can mount it, unmount it, rerender it, or throw the DOM node away—we already have our copy.

A strong design would use three capture layers:


### 1. Network capture — strongest method

The ChatGPT web application has to obtain conversation information somehow in order to display it. A browser extension can run **inside your authenticated ChatGPT tab** and observe the conversation data that the page itself receives.

There are already current open-source implementations doing essentially this. One hooks `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` at page startup and captures conversation JSON before rendering; another retrieves the current conversation's metadata specifically to avoid losing virtualized messages. citeturn900398search3turn900398search0

This is preferable to reading rendered text because:

```text

        ↓

        ↓
virtualization
        ↓
DOM
        ↓

```

We're getting the data **before the problematic part**.

If ChatGPT decides to render only messages 137–149, that doesn't matter if we already captured messages 1–236 from the conversation data.

### 2. Hydration/DOM recorder — independent fallback

We should not trust an undocumented internal interface to remain unchanged forever.

So the extension also gets a second collector using:

- `MutationObserver`
- conversation/message IDs
- `data-message-author-role`
- automatic scrolling
- local deduplication
- IndexedDB persistence

As messages appear:

```text

→ save permanently

Message 2 appears
→ save permanently

...

ChatGPT deletes Message 1 from DOM
→ DON'T CARE

→ save permanently
```

This technique is also being used successfully by current ChatGPT exporters specifically because messages are virtualized. citeturn900398search5turn900398search10

The crucial difference from Ctrl+A is that **our storage only grows**.

ChatGPT's DOM can shrink.

Our archive doesn't.

### 3. Selection recording — useful, but secondary

Your original idea is absolutely implementable.

Then JavaScript listens for:

So we'd be trying to fight virtualization after it has already affected selection.

## Design v0.1 — Local Chat Archive Extractor

### Primary objective

Given an open ChatGPT conversation:

```text
https://chatgpt.com/c/<conversation-id>
```

press one button:

```text
[ ARCHIVE THIS CHAT ]
```

and get a verified local archive:

```text
chat-title/
├── conversation.json
├── conversation.md
├── conversation.txt
└── archive-manifest.json
```

No Ctrl+A.

No dragging.

No dependence on the entire conversation being rendered simultaneously.

No cloud service of ours.

No third-party server.

---

# 1. Capture architecture

I would lock this order in:

```text
             OPEN CHATGPT CONVERSATION
                       │
                       ▼
              identify conversation ID
                       │
                       ▼
              PRIMARY EXTRACTOR
                internal fetch
                       │
                  successful?
                  /         \
                YES          NO
                 │            │
                 │            ▼
                 │       DOM HYDRATOR
                 │    scroll/capture/cache
                 │            │
                 └──────┬─────┘
                        ▼
                  NORMALIZATION
                        │
                        ▼
                 RECONCILIATION
                        │
                        ▼
                 LOCAL DATABASE
                        │
             ┌──────────┼──────────┐
             ▼          ▼          ▼
           JSON      Markdown      TXT
             │
             └──────────┬──────────┘
                        ▼
                INTEGRITY MANIFEST
```

### Capture method A — internal conversation fetch

This is the preferred path.

The extension runs on `chatgpt.com`, where you're already authenticated, and asks ChatGPT for the conversation that the ChatGPT application itself is displaying.

Current exporters are already successfully doing this using the existing logged-in session. citeturn689374search0turn689374search2

That means a 2-million-character conversation doesn't need to exist in the DOM simultaneously.

### Capture method B — DOM hydration

This is our fallback.

If OpenAI changes the internal endpoint or response format:

```text
scroll upward
↓
message appears
↓
record it permanently
↓
scroll
↓
another message appears
↓
record it permanently
```

Once recorded, unmounting doesn't matter.

This also gives us an independent source against which to compare the internal-data extraction.

---

# 2. Selection capture stays, but it is NOT the archive mechanism

I still like your original idea as a separate function:

```text
[ CAPTURE SELECTION ]
```

You highlight anything you want.

The extension immediately stores it.

Useful for things like:

```text
"This part belongs to Project X."
```

or:

```text
"I specifically need these 12 exchanges."
```

But:

> **selection recording will never be required to archive a complete conversation.**

That's now a locked design decision.

---

# 3. Persistent local capture

We should not build a giant in-memory JavaScript object and hope Chrome stays alive.

Captured messages get persisted incrementally.

Chrome currently supports IndexedDB from extension service workers. Importantly, Chrome's documentation says that web-storage calls made directly from a content script belong to the host page rather than the extension, so our content script should send captured records back to the extension service worker and store them under the **extension's own origin**. citeturn323435search2turn323435search5

Architecture:

```text
ChatGPT page
     │
content script
     │
chrome.runtime.sendMessage()
     │
extension service worker
     │
     ▼
IndexedDB

conversation abc123
├── metadata
├── msg001
├── msg002
├── msg003
├── ...
└── capture-state
```

So if Chrome crashes at message 927:

```text
927 messages remain saved.
```

Reopen:

```text
Archive found.

Captured: 927
Resume capture?
```

---

# 4. User-visible content boundary

This needs to be explicit.

The exporter is intended to preserve:

- your prompts
- assistant responses shown to you
- visible code blocks
- visible citations/links
- visible tool/result content where appropriate
- conversation title
- timestamps where available
- message IDs
- parent/child relationships
- branch information
- user-uploaded attachment references
- generated artifact references that were shown in the conversation

It should **not attempt to harvest hidden system/developer instructions, hidden reasoning, authentication credentials, session tokens, cookies, or other non-user-visible internal data**.

That also means I don't want to simply dump every byte returned by an internal endpoint onto disk.

Instead:

```text
internal response
       │
       ▼
 visibility + safety filter
       │
       ▼
canonical archive
```

This gives us the content you actually need without creating a giant credential/privacy hazard.

---

# 5. Preserve structure before rendering Markdown

This is important.

We should **not immediately flatten everything to text**.

Canonical JSON first:

```json
{
  "schema_version": "1.0",
  "conversation": {
    "id": "abc123",
    "title": "Movie Library Cataloging"
  },
  "messages": [
    {
      "id": "msg001",
      "parent_id": null,
      "role": "user",
      "content": [
        {
          "type": "text",
          "text": "..."
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "msg002",
      "parent_id": "msg001",
      "role": "assistant",
      "content": [
        {
          "type": "text",
          "text": "..."
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Then:

```text
canonical JSON
      │
      ├──> Markdown
      ├──> TXT
      ├──> project-context extractor later
      └──> search/index later
```

That protects us from throwing useful structural information away.

---

# 6. Branches must be preserved

ChatGPT conversations aren't necessarily simple linear lists.

You can regenerate an answer, edit prompts, branch conversations, etc.

Internally you can have something closer to:

```text
User A
  │
Assistant B
  │
User C
  ├───────────────┐
  ▼               ▼
Assistant D1    Assistant D2
                  │
                  ▼
                User E
```

The archive should therefore preserve:

```text
message ID
parent ID
children
branch relationships
```

For the readable Markdown:

> Export the branch currently displayed to you.

For canonical JSON:

> Preserve all **user-visible branches we can establish**, rather than destroying them by flattening prematurely.

---

# 7. Reconciliation

This is one of the most useful pieces.

Suppose internal fetch says:

```text
412 messages
```

DOM hydration observes:

```text
412 messages
```

And every DOM-visible message maps to a captured message ID/content hash.

Then:

```text
CAPTURE STATUS: VERIFIED
```

But suppose:

```text
Internal: 412
DOM:      407
```

We don't automatically declare failure because virtualization may explain it.

Instead:

```text
Internal source: COMPLETE
DOM validation: PARTIAL
Missing from DOM validation: 5

Archive confidence: HIGH
```

Or:

```text
Internal fetch: FAILED
DOM capture: 407
Unable to establish expected total.

Archive confidence: PARTIAL
```

Never silently call something complete when we cannot prove it.

Every archive gets:

```text
archive-manifest.json
```

Containing something approximately like:

```json
{

  "capture_method": [
    "internal_fetch",
    "dom_reconciliation"

    "status": "verified"

    "conversation.json": {
      "sha256": "..."
    },

      "sha256": "..."
    },
    "conversation.txt": {
      "sha256": "..."
    }
  }
}
```

This is particularly useful later when we're feeding recovered conversations into another pipeline.

We know exactly which archive was used.

I want this extension deliberately constrained.

Initially:

```text

https://chatgpt.com/*
```

Not:


No reason for it to read Gmail, GitHub, banking sites, etc.

- Google Analytics

- npm-delivered runtime dependency

- update server of ours

# 12. MVP scope

I think we should deliberately prevent feature creep for version `0.1`.

### Must have

1. Detect currently open ChatGPT conversation.
2. Determine conversation ID.
3. Fetch complete user-visible conversation data.
4. Normalize message structure.
5. Preserve message IDs/relationships.
6. Store capture locally.
7. Resume interrupted capture.
8. Export JSON.
9. Export Markdown.
10. Export TXT.
11. Calculate hashes.
12. Produce integrity manifest.
13. DOM reconciliation/fallback.
14. Never transmit archive externally.

### Explicitly later

- entire-account export
- project-wide batch export
- automatic attachment downloads
- search
- tagging
- classification
- Git integration
- GACP integration
- automatic project detection
- context summarization
- Chrome overlay
- Firefox support
- other AI sites
- automatic scheduled archival

That distinction should keep the first version small enough that we can actually **start extracting chats quickly**.

> **A capture is successful only when the extractor can produce a local archive containing the complete user-visible conversation independently of Chrome's native text-selection behavior, with sufficient metadata to establish ordering and identity and an integrity report describing how completeness was established.**

That is the core requirement.

```bash
        }

        const conversationId = match[1];

        /*
         * Obtain the short-lived access token from the same authenticated
         * ChatGPT browser session.
         *
         * IMPORTANT:
         * The token never leaves this function, is never logged, and is
         * never written into the exported archive.
         */
        const sessionResponse = await fetch("/api/auth/session", {
          method: "GET",
          credentials: "include",
          cache: "no-store"
        });

        if (!sessionResponse.ok) {
          throw new Error(
            `Session request failed: HTTP ${sessionResponse.status}`
          );
        }

        const session = await sessionResponse.json();
        const token = session?.accessToken;

        if (!token) {
          throw new Error(
            "ChatGPT session did not provide an access token."
          );
        }

        const deviceId = crypto.randomUUID();

        const response = await fetch(
          `/backend-api/conversation/${encodeURIComponent(conversationId)}`,
          {
            method: "GET",
            credentials: "include",
            cache: "no-store",
            headers: {
              "Accept": "application/json",
              "Authorization": `Bearer ${token}`,
              "Oai-Device-Id": deviceId,
              "Oai-Language": "en-US"
            }
          }
        );

        if (!response.ok) {
          const body = await response.text().catch(() => "");

          throw new Error(
            `Conversation request failed: HTTP ${response.status}` +
            (body ? ` — ${body.slice(0, 200)}` : "")
          );
        }

        const conversation = await response.json();

        /*
         * Do not retain token/session material.
         * Only the conversation API response is exported.
         */
        const raw = JSON.stringify(conversation, null, 2);

        const mapping = conversation?.mapping || {};

        let messages = 0;
        let userMessages = 0;
        let assistantMessages = 0;
        let systemMessages = 0;
        let visibleTextCharacters = 0;

        for (const node of Object.values(mapping)) {
          const message = node?.message;

          if (!message) {
            continue;
          }

          messages++;

          const role = message?.author?.role;

          if (role === "user") {
            userMessages++;
          } else if (role === "assistant") {
            assistantMessages++;
          } else if (role === "system") {
            systemMessages++;
          }

          const parts = message?.content?.parts;

          if (Array.isArray(parts)) {
            for (const part of parts) {
              if (typeof part === "string") {
                visibleTextCharacters += part.length;
              }
            }
          }
        }

        const title = conversation?.title || "Untitled Chat";

        const filename =
          `${safeFilename(title)}_${conversationId}.raw.json`;

        const blob = new Blob(
          [raw],
          {
            type: "application/json;charset=utf-8"
          }
        );

        const objectUrl = URL.createObjectURL(blob);

        const anchor = document.createElement("a");

        anchor.href = objectUrl;
        anchor.download = filename;
        anchor.style.display = "none";

        document.body.appendChild(anchor);
        anchor.click();
        anchor.remove();

        setTimeout(() => {
          URL.revokeObjectURL(objectUrl);
        }, 30000);

        return {
          ok: true,
          conversationId,
          title,
          mappingNodes: Object.keys(mapping).length,
          messages,
          userMessages,
          assistantMessages,
          systemMessages,
          visibleTextCharacters,
          rawJsonCharacters: raw.length,
          filename
        };
      }
    });

    const result = results?.[0]?.result;

    if (!result?.ok) {
      throw new Error("Extractor returned no result.");
    }

    setStatus(
      [
        "EXTRACTION SUCCEEDED",
        "",
        `Title: ${result.title}`,
        `Conversation: ${result.conversationId}`,
        "",
        `Mapping nodes: ${result.mappingNodes}`,
        `Messages: ${result.messages}`,
        `User: ${result.userMessages}`,
        `Assistant: ${result.assistantMessages}`,
        `System/internal nodes: ${result.systemMessages}`,
        "",
        `Visible text chars: ${result.visibleTextCharacters.toLocaleString()}`,
        `Raw JSON chars: ${result.rawJsonCharacters.toLocaleString()}`,
        "",
        `Downloaded:`,
        result.filename
      ].join("\n")
    );

  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);

    setStatus(
      `EXTRACTION FAILED\n\n${error?.message || String(error)}`
    );
  } finally {
    button.disabled = false;
  }
});
```
