# Local Chat Archive Extractor — Design v0.0.1

## Objective

Prove that a complete ChatGPT conversation can be extracted independently
of browser text selection and DOM virtualization.

## Critical Requirement

The proof must successfully retrieve structured conversation data for a
conversation that cannot be completely copied using Ctrl+A / Ctrl+C.

## Capture Method

v0.0.1 uses the authenticated ChatGPT browser session.

1. Identify the conversation ID from the current `/c/<id>` URL.
2. Request the short-lived browser-session access token.
3. Request `/backend-api/conversation/<id>`.
4. Keep the token only in JavaScript memory for the duration of the request.
5. Export only the returned conversation object.
6. Download the raw JSON locally.

## Security Boundaries

v0.0.1:

- has no permanent site permission;
- uses Chrome `activeTab` permission;
- runs only after an explicit extension-button click;
- refuses to operate outside `https://chatgpt.com`;
- does not persist access tokens;
- does not persist cookies;
- does not transmit extracted data externally;
- does not modify conversations;
- performs only GET requests;
- does not use telemetry or analytics.

## Canonical Proof Artifact

`<title>_<conversation-id>.raw.json`

This is intentionally the unnormalized conversation response.

Normalization, Markdown, TXT, integrity manifests, IndexedDB persistence,
DOM reconciliation, selection capture, and resumable archives belong to
later milestones.

## v0.0.1 Acceptance Criteria

PASS requires:

1. Extension loads as an unpacked Manifest V3 extension.
2. A normal ChatGPT conversation is detected.
3. Session authentication succeeds without manual token copying.
4. Full conversation endpoint returns HTTP 200.
5. Raw conversation JSON downloads locally.
6. JSON contains a `mapping` object.
7. Message counts are reported.
8. The test succeeds on a long conversation whose entire contents cannot be
   recovered with Ctrl+A / Ctrl+C.
9. No authentication token appears in the downloaded JSON as a result of
   extractor-added metadata.

## Non-Goals

v0.0.1 does not:

- determine archive completeness cryptographically;
- filter user-visible versus non-visible message nodes;
- normalize the conversation schema;
- render Markdown;
- render TXT;
- download attachments;
- store archives in IndexedDB;
- resume interrupted archives;
- capture multiple chats;
- integrate with Git or GACP;
- automatically classify project context.

Those capabilities begin only after the extraction proof passes.
EOF

            "Good. Then we do this as a proper adapter layer, not a hack.\n\nLocked target, unchanged from your hand-off:\n\n**Open WebUI → orchestrator → local AI → ChatGPT → final response → Open WebUI** fileciteturn0file0L21-L41\n\nAnd the hard rules stay locked:\n\n- no UI message injection\n- no replaying agent messages into rooms\n- no undocumented Open WebUI chat-state control\n- only one final response returned to the UI fileciteturn0file0L42-L68\n\nSo “right from the beginning” means this:\n\n## What we are building\n\nA **single OpenAI-compatible inference gateway** that Open WebUI treats like its model backend.\n\nOpen WebUI will send a normal chat completion request to the orchestrator.\nThe orchestrator will:\n\n1. extract the user message\n2. call local AI first\n3. call ChatGPT second, using the local draft\n4. enforce strict output contract\n5. return one final assistant response to Open WebUI\n\nNo separate speakers in UI.\nNo agent chatter in UI.\nNo half-step architecture.\n\n## What “done correctly” requires\n\nWe should build this as four files, not one blob:\n\n1. `main.py`\n   FastAPI app exposing `/v1/chat/completions` and `/health`\n\n2. `schemas.py`\n   Request/response models for OpenAI-compatible input/output\n\n3. `orchestrator.py`\n   Core execution flow:\n   `user -> local -> chatgpt -> final`\n\n4. `providers.py`\n   Provider clients:\n   - Ollama local model client\n   - OpenAI client for ChatGPT\n\nAnd one settings file:\n\n5. `config.py`\n   All URLs, model names, timeouts, strict-mode flags from env\n\nThat gives you a real service boundary instead of a throwaway script.\n\n## Non-negotiable behavior\n\nFor the locked test case:\n\nInput:\n```text\nrun test suite\n```\n\nOutput:\n```json\n{\n  \"objective\": \"run test suite\",\n  \"steps\": [\n    { \"action_type\": \"run_pytest\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nNo explanation text.\nNo questions.\nNo conversational filler. fileciteturn0file0L69-L92\n\n## Correct implementation doctrine\n\nThe orchestrator should do all of this from day one:\n\n- strict JSON-only finalization\n- deterministic prompts\n- zero-temperature final pass\n- explicit fallback when local output is garbage\n- no dependence on Open WebUI internals\n- OpenAI-compatible response shape so WebUI can use it directly\n\n## What I will not do in this chat\n\nI will not send you:\n- another terminal relay\n- another room injection attempt\n- another “temporary starter”\n- another “we’ll fix it later” version\n\n## Build order\n\nThis is the right order:\n\n1. define the gateway contract\n2. implement provider clients\n3. implement orchestration logic\n4. expose `/v1/chat/completions`\n5. wire Open WebUI’s OpenAI connection to this service\n6. test only through Open WebUI\n\n## Next step\n\nI’m going to give you the full initial file set as **complete replacements**, not fragments:\n\n- `config.py`\n- `schemas.py`\n- `providers.py`\n- `orchestrator.py`\n- `main.py`\n- `requirements.txt`\n\nAssumptions I’m locking unless you tell me otherwise:\n\n- orchestrator runs on the XPS\n- Ollama stays at `http://192.168.1.253:11434`\n- Open WebUI will point its OpenAI base URL to the orchestrator\n- final output is returned as plain assistant text containing strict JSON\n- first supported action is `run_pytest`\n\nIf that lock is acceptable, I’ll produce the full file set in the next message."

            "Yes—**if we build those controls into the gateway**, that architecture supports exactly that.\n\nBut I want to be precise about what is already implied by the design versus what must be explicitly implemented.\n\n## What this architecture can support\n\nBehind one Open WebUI request, the gateway can enforce:\n\n- **local AI goes first**\n- **ChatGPT goes second**\n- **max turn budget**\n- **structured final output only**\n- **user remains authority**\n\nSo a bounded flow like this is straightforward:\n\n1. user sends message\n2. local AI reply #1\n3. ChatGPT reply #1\n4. optional local AI reply #2\n5. optional ChatGPT reply #2\n6. stop and return final result\n\nThat gives you the **2 messages per AI** cap you want.\n\n## What “interrupt anytime” means in practice\n\nThere are two different meanings:\n\n### 1. Between requests\nThis is easy and clean.\n\nYou send a new message like:\n- stop\n- revise\n- ignore previous\n- do this instead\n\nThe next orchestration cycle obeys you.\n\n### 2. Mid-flight during one running request\nThis is **possible**, but only if we explicitly build cancellation support into the gateway.\n\nThat means:\n- request gets a run/session ID\n- gateway tracks active run state\n- user can issue a cancel/interruption action\n- gateway stops after current provider call or timeout boundary\n\nSo “interrupt anytime” is not automatic just because we have a gateway. It is a **feature we must implement intentionally**.\n\n## What “approve when necessary” means\n\nSame answer: yes, but only if we make approval a first-class gate.\n\nThat means the gateway can enforce states like:\n\n- draft only\n- awaiting user approval\n- approved to continue\n- blocked / cancelled\n\nSo the system can absolutely be designed so that certain outputs do **not** auto-complete without your approval.\n\n## The important boundary\n\nOpen WebUI itself is **not** managing this logic.\n\nThe **gateway** manages:\n- turn limits\n- ordering\n- stop conditions\n- approval gates\n- final response contract\n\nOpen WebUI is only the front end.\n\n## The honest answer\n\nSo the answer is:\n\n- **Yes**, this architecture is the right one for that behavior.\n- **No**, those controls do not appear by magic just because we route through a gateway.\n- We need to build them deliberately from the start, which is exactly what we should do.\n\n## What this means for the build\n\nWe should treat these as locked gateway requirements:\n\n- local AI first\n- ChatGPT second\n- max 2 messages per AI per cycle\n- user can stop / redirect\n- approval gate when required\n- one final UI response only\n\nIf you want that locked, then before `config.py` we should define the gateway contract around those controls first, so we do not build the wrong interface."

# Step 18 — Minimum Viable System (MVS)

## Objective

Design the smallest possible implementation capable of processing **one real chat** through the complete governance lifecycle:

```text
RECEIVED
↓
REGISTERED
↓
EXTRACTED
↓
REVIEWED
↓
ROUTED
↓
ARCHIVED
```

while preserving all currently locked governance decisions.

---

# MVS Design Principles

The MVS exists to validate governance, not automation.

The goal is **not**:

- bulk ingestion
- automation
- scalability
- ecosystem discovery at scale

The goal is:

> Can one chat be processed correctly under governance rules?

If yes:

- schemas can be tested
- SOP can be tested
- audit trail can be tested
- overlap handling can be tested
- human review can be tested

---

# MVS Scope Boundary

Included:

- One chat
- Manual review
- Local storage
- JSON artifacts
- Audit trail

Excluded:

- Batch processing
- Search engine
- Embeddings
- LLM automation
- Database
- UI
- Web application
- Multi-user support

---

# Minimum Repository Structure

```text
chat_sorter/

├── chats/
│   └── incoming/
│
├── artifacts/
│   ├── extraction_reports/
│   ├── routing_packets/
│   └── canonical_artifacts/
│
├── reviews/
│
├── archive/
│
├── manifests/
│
├── schemas/
│
├── scripts/
│
└── README.md
```

Nothing else is required for MVS.

---

# Required Schemas

Only schemas required to process one chat.

```text
schemas/

chat_manifest.schema.json

extraction_report.schema.json

routing_packet.schema.json

canonical_artifact.schema.json
```

All other schemas remain conceptual until needed.

---

# Required Scripts

Only four scripts.

## 1. register_chat.py

Purpose:

```text
Incoming Chat
↓
Assign Chat ID
↓
Create Manifest Entry
```

Produces:

```text
chat_manifest.json
```

---

## 2. create_extraction.py

Purpose:

Create initial extraction report.

Produces:

```text
extraction_report.json
```

Initially this can be human-generated and merely validated.

---

## 3. validate_artifact.py

Purpose:

Validate any artifact against schema.

Used on:

- manifest
- extraction report
- routing packet
- canonical artifact

---

## 4. archive_chat.py

Purpose:

Move completed chat package into archive state.

Creates immutable archive record.

---

# First Chat Processing Workflow

## Stage 1 — Receive

Human selects one chat.

Example:

```text
ChatGPT Recents

Website Revision Strategy
```

Raw chat exported.

Stored:

```text
chats/incoming/
```

Raw chat is immutable evidence.

---

## Stage 2 — Register

Run:

```bash
python register_chat.py
```

Produces:

```json
{
  "chat_id": "CHAT-000001",
  "status": "REGISTERED"
}
```

Manifest updated.

---

## Stage 3 — Extract

Human performs extraction.

Produces:

```json
{
  "chat_id": "CHAT-000001",
  "candidate_projects": [],
  "candidate_artifacts": [],
  "candidate_concepts": [],
  "candidate_overlaps": []
}
```

Stored:

```text
artifacts/extraction_reports/
```

No routing yet.

No interpretation yet.

Only extraction.

---

## Stage 4 — Review

Human reviews extraction.

Possible outcomes:

```text
APPROVED
REJECTED
NEEDS_REVISION
UNKNOWN
```

Stored:

```text
reviews/
```

This is the first authoritative decision point.

---

## Stage 5 — Route

After approval:

Routing packet created.

Example:

```json
{
  "artifact_id": "ART-000001",
  "routing_destination": "TranslAItor",
  "routing_reason": "Evidence supports relevance"
}
```

Important:

Routing destination is not ownership.

Locked governance remains intact.

---

## Stage 6 — Archive

Run:

```bash
python archive_chat.py
```

Archive package contains:

```text
raw_chat
manifest
extraction_report
review_record
routing_packet
```

Stored:

```text
archive/
```

Chat becomes immutable historical evidence.

---

# Minimum Review Record

New artifact required.

```text
reviews/review_record.json
```

Contains:

```json
{
  "review_id": "REV-000001",
  "chat_id": "CHAT-000001",
  "review_status": "APPROVED",
  "reviewer": "human",
  "timestamp": "..."
}
```

This is necessary because human review authority is locked governance.

Without it:

Review authority cannot be audited.

---

# Minimum Manifest Contents

Manifest only needs:

```json
{
  "chat_id": "CHAT-000001",
  "source_location": "ChatGPT Recents",
  "received_timestamp": "...",
  "lifecycle_state": "REGISTERED"
}
```

Nothing more is required.

---

# Success Criteria

The MVS succeeds if one chat can produce:

```text
Raw Chat
✓

Manifest
✓

Extraction Report
✓

Review Record
✓

Routing Packet
✓

Archive Record
✓
```

and every artifact can be validated against schema.

---

# MVS Deliverable

At completion, the repository should be capable of answering:

> "Show me every decision made about this chat and the evidence supporting it."

using only:

```text
raw_chat
manifest
extraction_report
review_record
routing_packet
archive_record
```

If that question can be answered completely, the governance model has survived first contact with reality.

That constitutes a valid Step 18 MVS under all currently locked project constraints.

            "Yes. You should be able to extract the text from a conversation without depending on click-and-drag selection in the ChatGPT UI.\n\nI also would not assume the behavior you’re seeing is necessarily an intentional “you may only copy X characters” policy. Very long ChatGPT conversations use a fairly complicated frontend, and rendering/virtualization can interfere with browser selection. Either way, the practical result is the same: **the UI should not be the only way you can retrieve your own conversation text.**\n\n### Fast workaround in Chrome\n\nFor an existing conversation, open the conversation, press **F12**, select **Console**, and run this:\n\n```javascript\n(() => {\n  const messages = [...document.querySelectorAll('[data-message-author-role]')];\n\n  const text = messages.map((el, i) => {\n    const role = el.getAttribute('data-message-author-role') || 'unknown';\n\n    return [\n      `===== MESSAGE ${i + 1} — ${role.toUpperCase()} =====`,\n      el.innerText.trim()\n    ].join('\\n');\n  }).join('\\n\\n');\n\n  copy(text);\n\n  console.log(\n    `Copied ${text.length.toLocaleString()} characters from ${messages.length} messages.`\n  );\n})();\n```\n\nThat does **not highlight anything**. It reads the conversation text directly from the page DOM and puts it on your clipboard.\n\nSo if Chrome's visual selection craps out at, say, 100,000 characters, that limitation is irrelevant to this method.\n\nThere is one important caveat: **very long conversations may be virtualized**. In that case, ChatGPT may remove older messages from the DOM while you're looking at newer ones. If the console reports something suspicious like:\n\n> Copied 84,321 characters from 17 messages\n\nwhen you know the conversation contains 200 messages, then we've hit virtualization rather than a clipboard limit.\n\n### For enormous chats, I would build around virtualization\n\nWe can make a slightly more sophisticated Chrome script that:\n\n1. finds the ChatGPT conversation's scroll container;\n2. starts at the top;\n3. walks downward through the entire conversation;\n4. captures each user/assistant message as ChatGPT renders it;\n5. deduplicates messages that appear during overlapping scroll positions;\n6. reconstructs the whole conversation;\n7. copies it to the clipboard **or downloads it as Markdown/text/JSON**.\n\nThat would effectively give you a **\"Rip this entire ChatGPT conversation out of the webpage\"** function.\n\nAnd unlike the normal selection mechanism, there would be no meaningful character limit other than browser memory.\n\n### There is also an official bulk-recovery path\n\nOpenAI currently provides **Settings → Data controls → Export data**. The resulting ZIP includes your chat history. OpenAI says exports can take up to seven days, so that's useful as an archival/backstop mechanism, but not as a practical tool when you're sitting in a chat and need its contents right now. citeturn888753search3turn888753search6\n\nFor what you're doing with preserving old project conversations and recovering project context, I think the better solution is actually the browser extractor rather than depending on export.           "content_type": "text",
          "parts": [
            "Yes. What you are describing is real, and I found the mechanism behind it.\n\nIt is **not primarily Chrome running out of clipboard memory**. ChatGPT's web interface is **virtualizing/windowing long conversations**. In a sufficiently long thread, only a small portion of the conversation exists in the browser's DOM at any one time. As you scroll, older messages are actually **removed from the DOM** and different messages are mounted in their place. A recent OpenAI community report describes exactly this behavior, and OpenAI Support acknowledged the underlying long-conversation problem. citeturn725644search8turn725644search11\n\nThat explains both things you're seeing:\n\n- **Ctrl+A → Ctrl+C:** it cannot copy messages that aren't currently instantiated in the webpage.\n- **Start highlighting at the top and drag all the way down:** while you travel downward, the frontend can unmount portions you already passed. Your selection therefore cannot remain attached to one giant continuous body of text.\n\nSo yes: **from your perspective, ChatGPT is preventing the browser from copying the whole damn chat.** The important correction is only *how* it is happening. It isn't necessarily a fixed `100,000-character clipboard limit`; the page is refusing to keep the whole conversation resident in the DOM simultaneously.\n\nInterestingly, OpenAI's current release notes specifically advertise improved `Ctrl+A` behavior intended to select conversation content, but long-thread virtualization can still defeat that because unmounted content isn't available to browser selection in the first place. citeturn725644search7turn725644search11\n\n### The workaround I think we should use\n\n**Stop using browser text selection entirely.**\n\nThere are already working tools using two approaches that prove this is feasible.\n\nOne current Chrome extension, **ChatGPT Thread Exporter**, explicitly says it was designed for ChatGPT's dynamically mounted conversations introduced in 2026 and **reads the conversation data model rather than relying on Ctrl+A**. citeturn725644search10\n\nAnother current script handles virtualization by automatically scrolling through the entire conversation, capturing each message while it becomes mounted, deduplicating messages by ID, and ultimately producing a Markdown file. It was tested against the 2026 ChatGPT interface. citeturn725644search15\n\nThere's also a more comprehensive open-source exporter that retrieves conversations through the authenticated browser session and produces both raw JSON and Markdown. citeturn725644search6\n\nFor **your use case**, I would not make clipboard copy the primary output at all.\n\nI'd build a small local Chrome userscript/extension that gives you something like:\n\n```text\nExport Chat\n```\n\nWhen pressed:\n\n```text\nConversation detected\n↓\nwalk entire conversation\n↓\ncapture every user message\ncapture every assistant message\ncapture code blocks\ncapture links\ncapture timestamps/IDs where available\n↓\nverify message count\n↓\nSAVE\n```\n\nAnd produce:\n\n```text\nMovie_Library_Cataloging_2026-08-25.md\nMovie_Library_Cataloging_2026-08-25.json\n```\n\nThen optionally:\n\n```text\nCOPY ALL\n```\n\nfrom **our reconstructed copy**, not ChatGPT's DOM.\n\nThat distinction matters. Once we've reconstructed the conversation ourselves, OpenAI's frontend virtualization is irrelevant.\n\n### Even better for what you're doing\n\nBecause you're recovering enormous old project chats, I think we should make this a proper local tool rather than some disposable console snippet.\n\nIt could have:\n\n```text\n[ Export Current Chat ]\n[ Copy Entire Chat ]\n[ Save Markdown ]\n[ Save Raw JSON ]\n\nMessages found:       347\nUser messages:        174\nAssistant messages:   173\nCharacters:           1,847,392\n\nCapture status: COMPLETE\n```\n\nAnd I would make **the file the authoritative artifact**, not the clipboard.\n\nThen a 2-million-character conversation, 5-million-character conversation, whatever, isn't dependent upon:\n\n- DOM virtualization\n- text-selection behavior\n- Ctrl+A\n- clipboard UI\n- dragging for twenty fucking minutes\n- whether ChatGPT decides to unmount the top half while you're selecting the bottom half\n\nThe official OpenAI export remains a fallback and does include chat history, but it can take **up to seven days**, so it is completely inappropriate for \"I need this conversation right now.\" citeturn725644search2\n\nSo I think we have identified the right problem now: **we need to bypass ChatGPT's rendered conversation layer altogether, not figure out how to make Chrome select more text.**\n\nAnd given the amount of old project context you're trying to recover, I think building our own **local ChatGPT Conversation Extractor** is worth doing rather than trusting a third-party extension. memcite"

        "content": {
          "content_type": "text",
          "parts": [
            "The **best method is not to record the highlight**. We can do that, but it still leaves OpenAI's virtualized DOM in control of what exists at any instant.\n\nI would build the extractor so that **the moment any part of the conversation becomes available to the browser, we permanently cache it locally**. After that, ChatGPT can mount it, unmount it, rerender it, or throw the DOM node away—we already have our copy.\n\nA strong design would use three capture layers:\n\n```text\n                    CHATGPT TAB\n                        │\n        ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐\n        ▼               ▼                ▼\n   Network/API      DOM Observer     Selection Recorder\n     Capture        + Auto-scroll       optional\n        │               │                │\n        └───────────────┼────────────────┘\n                        ▼\n                  LOCAL MESSAGE DB\n                    IndexedDB\n                        │\n              ┌─────────┼─────────┐\n              ▼         ▼         ▼\n            JSON     Markdown    TXT\n              │\n              ▼\n        completeness report\n```\n\n### 1. Network capture — strongest method\n\nThe ChatGPT web application has to obtain conversation information somehow in order to display it. A browser extension can run **inside your authenticated ChatGPT tab** and observe the conversation data that the page itself receives.\n\nThere are already current open-source implementations doing essentially this. One hooks `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` at page startup and captures conversation JSON before rendering; another retrieves the current conversation's metadata specifically to avoid losing virtualized messages. citeturn900398search3turn900398search0\n\nThis is preferable to reading rendered text because:\n\n```text\nServer conversation data\n        ↓\nOUR LOCAL COPY  ← capture here\n        ↓\nChatGPT frontend\n        ↓\nvirtualization\n        ↓\nDOM\n        ↓\nCtrl+A / highlighting\n```\n\nWe're getting the data **before the problematic part**.\n\nIf ChatGPT decides to render only messages 137–149, that doesn't matter if we already captured messages 1–236 from the conversation data.\n\n### 2. Hydration/DOM recorder — independent fallback\n\nWe should not trust an undocumented internal interface to remain unchanged forever.\n\nSo the extension also gets a second collector using:\n\n- `MutationObserver`\n- conversation/message IDs\n- `data-message-author-role`\n- automatic scrolling\n- local deduplication\n- IndexedDB persistence\n\nAs messages appear:\n\n```text\nMessage 1 appears\n→ save permanently\n\nMessage 2 appears\n→ save permanently\n\n...\n\nChatGPT deletes Message 1 from DOM\n→ DON'T CARE\n\nMessage 28 appears\n→ save permanently\n```\n\nThis technique is also being used successfully by current ChatGPT exporters specifically because messages are virtualized. citeturn900398search5turn900398search10\n\nThe crucial difference from Ctrl+A is that **our storage only grows**.\n\nChatGPT's DOM can shrink.\n\nOur archive doesn't.\n\n### 3. Selection recording — useful, but secondary\n\nYour original idea is absolutely implementable.\n\nWe could have a mode:\n\n```text\n[ ARM SELECTION CAPTURE ]\n```\n\nThen JavaScript listens for:\n\n```javascript\nselectionchange\nmouseup\npointerup\n```\n\nand reads:\n\n```javascript\nwindow.getSelection().toString()\n```\n\nEach completed selection could immediately be copied into our local buffer.\n\nSo:\n\n```text\nYou highlight paragraph A\n→ saved\n\nYou continue\n→ paragraph B saved\n\nDOM deletes paragraph A\n→ paragraph A remains in our database\n```\n\nWe could even show:\n\n```text\nSELECTION CAPTURE\n\nChunks captured:       47\nCharacters captured:   283,441\nUnique characters:     278,912\nStatus: RECORDING\n```\n\nBut I **would not rely on continuous drag-selection**. selection.\n\nBetter:\n\n> **Observe the conversation, not the highlight.**\n\nSelection capture becomes useful for grabbing **specific portions** of conversations rather than recovering the complete 2,814,922\n\nCapture methods:\n✓ Conversation data\n✓ DOM hydration\n✓ Local cache\n\nIntegrity:\n✓ no duplicate IDs\n✓ sequence reconstructed\n✓ export generated\n\n[ EXPORT MARKDOWN ]\n[ EXPORT JSON ┌──────┼──────┐\n   ▼      ▼      ▼\n JSON     MD     TXT\n```\n\n### The archive should be resumable\n\nThis is particularly important.\n\nSuppose you have a monstrous chat and Chrome crashes halfway contain a report like:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"conversation_id\": \"abc123\",\n  \"title\": \"Movie Library Cataloging\",\n\n  \"capture\": {\n    \"messages\": 386,\n    \"user_messages\": 193,\n    \"assistant_messages\": 193\n  },\n\n  \"validation\": {\n    \"duplicate_message_ids\": 0,\n    \"missing_parent_links\": 0,\n    \"unresolved_messages\": 0,\n    \"capture_complete\": true\n  }\n}\n```\n\nAnd calculate hashes:\n\n```text\nconversation.json\nSHA-256: 5a742...\n\nconversation.md\nSHA-256: ae137...\n```\n\nNow we don't merely have **a copy**.\n\nWe have a locally verifiable archival artifact.\n\n---\n\n## I would also intentionally restrict the extension\n\nSince conversations can contain private information, I would make our extension rather paranoid:\n\n```text\nPermissions:\n    chatgpt.com ONLY\n\nExternal network access:\n    NONE\n\nAnalytics:\n    NONE\n\nTelemetry:\n    NONE\n\nRemote code:\n    NONE\n\nCloud storage:\n    NONE\n\nAuthentication storage:\n    NONE\n\nCookies/tokens written to disk:\n    NEVER\n```\n\nIt can use your existing authenticated browser session, but we don't need to dump session cookies,             {
              "summary": "Freezing the MVP architecture",
              "content": "I’m minimizing permissions: capture from the visible chat page, store locally, export through a normal file download, and keep enrichment optional. I’m separating extraction, normalization, indexing, and project-note generation so later changes stay contained.",
              "chunks": [],
              "finished": true
            },
            {
              "summary": "Choosing persistence boundaries",
              "content": "I’m keeping page extraction lightweight and sending normalized records to the extension’s background layer for local persistence. That avoids mixing host-page storage with extension data and leaves room for large archives without complicating the first build.",
              "chunks": [],
              "finished": true
            },
            {
              "summary": "Defining extraction scope",
              "content": "I’m limiting capture to user-visible conversation content and user-owned attachments. I’m excluding hidden fields, using a stable canonical schema, and treating selection-based recording as optional rather than foundational.",
              "chunks": [],
              "finished": true

            "Yes. I think we have enough now to **freeze the core architecture** and move toward an MVP that we can actually use on your old chats.\n\nThe main design decision is this:\n\n> **We do not solve the problem by making browser selection better. We extract the conversation independently of selection.**\n\nCurrent open-source implementations confirm that the authenticated ChatGPT page can fetch complete conversation data through the existing browser session, including approaches that use ChatGPT's internal conversation endpoint rather than depending on the rendered DOM. citeturn689374search0turn689374search2\n\n## Design v0.1 — Local Chat Archive Extractor\n\n### Primary objective\n\nGiven an open ChatGPT conversation:\n\n```text\nhttps://chatgpt.com/c/<conversation-id>\n```\n\npress one button:\n\n```text\n[ ARCHIVE THIS CHAT ]\n```\n\nand get a verified local archive:\n\n```text\nchat-title/\n├── conversation.json\n├── conversation.md\n├── conversation.txt\n└── archive-manifest.json\n```\n\nNo Ctrl+A.\n\nNo dragging.\n\nNo dependence on the entire conversation being rendered simultaneously.\n\nNo cloud service of ours.\n\nNo third-party server.\n\n---\n\n# 1. Capture architecture\n\nI would lock this order in:\n\n```text\n             OPEN CHATGPT CONVERSATION\n                       │\n                       ▼\n              identify conversation ID\n                       │\n                       ▼\n              PRIMARY EXTRACTOR\n                internal fetch\n                       │\n                  successful?\n                  /         \\\n                YES          NO\n                 │            │\n                 │            ▼\n                 │       DOM HYDRATOR\n                 │    scroll/capture/cache\n                 │            │\n                 └──────┬─────┘\n                        ▼\n                  NORMALIZATION\n                        │\n                        ▼\n                 RECONCILIATION\n                        │\n                        ▼\n                 LOCAL DATABASE\n                        │\n             ┌──────────┼──────────┐\n             ▼          ▼          ▼\n           JSON      Markdown      TXT\n             │\n             └──────────┬──────────┘\n                        ▼\n                INTEGRITY MANIFEST\n```\n\n### Capture method A — internal conversation fetch\n\nThis is the preferred path.\n\nThe extension runs on `chatgpt.com`, where you're already authenticated, and asks ChatGPT for the conversation that the ChatGPT application itself is displaying.\n\nCurrent exporters are already successfully doing this using the existing logged-in session. citeturn689374search0turn689374search2\n\nThat means a 2-million-character conversation doesn't need to exist in the DOM simultaneously.\n\n### Capture method B — DOM hydration\n\nThis is our fallback.\n\nIf OpenAI changes the internal endpoint or response format:\n\n```text\nscroll upward\n↓\nmessage appears\n↓\nrecord it permanently\n↓\nscroll\n↓\nanother message appears\n↓\nrecord it permanently\n```\n\nOnce recorded, unmounting doesn't matter.\n\nThis also gives us an independent source against which to compare the internal-data extraction.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Selection capture stays, but it is NOT the archive mechanism\n\nI still like your original idea as a separate function:\n\n```text\n[ CAPTURE SELECTION ]\n```\n\nYou highlight anything you want.\n\nThe extension immediately stores it.\n\nUseful for things like:\n\n```text\n\"This part belongs to Project X.\"\n```\n\nor:\n\n```text\n\"I specifically need these 12 exchanges.\"\n```\n\nBut:\n\n> **selection recording will never be required to archive a complete conversation.**\n\nThat's now a locked design decision.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Persistent local capture\n\nWe should not build a giant in-memory JavaScript object and hope Chrome stays alive.\n\nCaptured messages get persisted incrementally.\n\nChrome currently supports IndexedDB from extension service workers. Importantly, Chrome's documentation says that web-storage calls made directly from a content script belong to the host page rather than the extension, so our content script should send captured records back to the extension service worker and store them under the **extension's own origin**. citeturn323435search2turn323435search5\n\nArchitecture:\n\n```text\nChatGPT page\n     │\ncontent script\n     │\nchrome.runtime.sendMessage()\n     │\nextension service worker\n     │\n     ▼\nIndexedDB\n\nconversation abc123\n├── metadata\n├── msg001\n├── msg002\n├── msg003\n├── ...\n└── capture-state\n```\n\nSo if Chrome crashes at message 927:\n\n```text\n927 messages remain saved.\n```\n\nReopen:\n\n```text\nArchive found.\n\nCaptured: 927\nResume capture?\n```\n\n---\n\n# 4. User-visible content boundary\n\nThis needs to be explicit.\n\nThe exporter is intended to preserve:\n\n- your prompts\n- assistant responses shown to you\n- visible code blocks\n- visible citations/links\n- visible tool/result content where appropriate\n- conversation title\n- timestamps where available\n- message IDs\n- parent/child relationships\n- branch information\n- user-uploaded attachment references\n- generated artifact references that were shown in the conversation\n\nIt should **not attempt to harvest hidden system/developer instructions, hidden reasoning, authentication credentials, session tokens, cookies, or other non-user-visible internal data**.\n\nThat also means I don't want to simply dump every byte returned by an internal endpoint onto disk.\n\nInstead:\n\n```text\ninternal response\n       │\n       ▼\n visibility + safety filter\n       │\n       ▼\ncanonical archive\n```\n\nThis gives us the content you actually need without creating a giant credential/privacy hazard.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Preserve structure before rendering Markdown\n\nThis is important.\n\nWe should **not immediately flatten everything to text**.\n\nCanonical JSON first:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"schema_version\": \"1.0\",\n  \"conversation\": {\n    \"id\": \"abc123\",\n    \"title\": \"Movie Library Cataloging\"\n  },\n  \"messages\": [\n    {\n      \"id\": \"msg001\",\n      \"parent_id\": null,\n      \"role\": \"user\",\n      \"content\": [\n        {\n          \"type\": \"text\",\n          \"text\": \"...\"\n        }\n      ]\n    },\n    {\n      \"id\": \"msg002\",\n      \"parent_id\": \"msg001\",\n      \"role\": \"assistant\",\n      \"content\": [\n        {\n          \"type\": \"text\",\n          \"text\": \"...\"\n        }\n      ]\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nThen:\n\n```text\ncanonical JSON\n      │\n      ├──> Markdown\n      ├──> TXT\n      ├──> project-context extractor later\n      └──> search/index later\n```\n\nThat protects us from throwing useful structural information away.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Branches must be preserved\n\nChatGPT conversations aren't necessarily simple linear lists.\n\nYou can regenerate an answer, edit prompts, branch conversations, etc.\n\nInternally you can have something closer to:\n\n```text\nUser A\n  │\nAssistant B\n  │\nUser C\n  ├───────────────┐\n  ▼               ▼\nAssistant D1    Assistant D2\n                  │\n                  ▼\n                User E\n```\n\nThe archive should therefore preserve:\n\n```text\nmessage ID\nparent ID\nchildren\nbranch relationships\n```\n\nFor the readable Markdown:\n\n> Export the branch currently displayed to you.\n\nFor canonical JSON:\n\n> Preserve all **user-visible branches we can establish**, rather than destroying them by flattening prematurely.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Reconciliation\n\nThis is one of the most useful pieces.\n\nSuppose internal fetch says:\n\n```text\n412 messages\n```\n\nDOM hydration observes:\n\n```text\n412 messages\n```\n\nAnd every DOM-visible message maps to a captured message ID/content hash.\n\nThen:\n\n```text\nCAPTURE STATUS: VERIFIED\n```\n\nBut suppose:\n\n```text\nInternal: 412\nDOM:      407\n```\n\nWe don't automatically declare failure because virtualization may explain it.\n\nInstead:\n\n```text\nInternal source: COMPLETE\nDOM validation: PARTIAL\nMissing from DOM validation: 5\n\nArchive confidence: HIGH\n```\n\nOr:\n\n```text\nInternal fetch: FAILED\nDOM capture: 407\nUnable to establish expected total.\n\nArchive confidence: PARTIAL\n```\n\nNever silently call something complete when we cannot prove it.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Integrity manifest\n\nEvery archive gets:\n\n```text\narchive-manifest.json\n```\n\nContaining something approximately like:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"schema_version\": \"1.0\",\n  \"capture_method\": [\n    \"internal_fetch\",\n    \"dom_reconciliation\"\n  ],\n  \"conversation_id\": \"abc123\",\n  \"message_count\": 412,\n  \"user_messages\": 206,\n  \"assistant_messages\": 206,\n  \"validation\": {\n    \"duplicate_ids\": 0,\n    \"unresolved_parent_links\": 0,\n    \"dom_messages_unmatched\": 0,\n    \"status\": \"verified\"\n  },\n  \"files\": {\n    \"conversation.json\": {\n      \"sha256\": \"...\"\n    },\n    \"conversation.md\": {\n      \"sha256\": \"...\"\n    },\n    \"conversation.txt\": {\n      \"sha256\": \"...\"\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThis is particularly useful later when we're feeding recovered conversations into another pipeline.\n\nWe know exactly which archive was used.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Minimal permissions\n\nI want this extension deliberately constrained.\n\nInitially:\n\n```text\nAllowed host:\n\nhttps://chatgpt.com/*\n```\n\nNot:\n\n```text\n<all_urls>\n```\n\nNo reason for it to read Gmail, GitHub, banking sites, etc.\n\nChrome allows content scripts to be restricted by URL match patterns. citeturn323435search0\n\nAnd I don't think MVP needs Chrome's `downloads` permission.\n\nThat permission produces a fairly broad **\"Manage your downloads\"** capability warning. citeturn678002search4turn678002search5\n\nInstead, we can initially create local Blob files and trigger ordinary browser downloads.\n\nFewer permissions.\n\nSmaller attack surface.\n\n---\n\n# 10. No external communications\n\nThis should be enforced architecturally:\n\n```text\nAllowed outbound destination:\n\nchatgpt.com\n```\n\nEverything else:\n\n```text\nDENY\n```\n\nNo:\n\n- telemetry\n- analytics\n- crash reporting service\n- Google Analytics\n- CDN libraries\n- npm-delivered runtime dependency\n- remote JavaScript\n- update server of ours\n- AI API\n- database server\n\nThe extension can be vanilla JS initially.\n\nCurrent ChatGPT exporter implementations demonstrate that a small local Manifest V3 extension is sufficient for the underlying extraction workflow. citeturn689374search0\n\n---\n\n# 11. UI\n\nMVP should stay extremely simple:\n\n```text\n┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│ LOCAL CHAT ARCHIVE                      │\n├─────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│                                         │\n│ Movie Library Cataloging                │\n│                                         │\n│ Conversation ID: abc123                 │\n│                                         │\n│ Captured:       412 messages            │\n│ Characters:     2,817,491               │\n│                                         │\n│ Internal fetch: ✓                       │\n│ DOM verified:   ✓                       │\n│ Integrity:      VERIFIED                │\n│                                         │\n│ [ ARCHIVE THIS CHAT ]                   │\n│                                         │\n│ [ JSON ] [ MARKDOWN ] [ TXT ]           │\n│                                         │\n│ [ CAPTURE SELECTION ]                   │\n│                                         │\n└─────────────────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nNo complicated settings screen initially.\n\n---\n\n# 12. MVP scope\n\nI think we should deliberately prevent feature creep for version `0.1`.\n\n### Must have\n\n1. Detect currently open ChatGPT conversation.\n2. Determine conversation ID.\n3. Fetch complete user-visible conversation data.\n4. Normalize message structure.\n5. Preserve message IDs/relationships.\n6. Store capture locally.\n7. Resume interrupted capture.\n8. Export JSON.\n9. Export Markdown.\n10. Export TXT.\n11. Calculate hashes.\n12. Produce integrity manifest.\n13. DOM reconciliation/fallback.\n14. Never transmit archive externally.\n\n### Explicitly later\n\n- entire-account export\n- project-wide batch export\n- automatic attachment downloads\n- search\n- tagging\n- classification\n- Git integration\n- GACP integration\n- automatic project detection\n- context summarization\n- Chrome overlay\n- Firefox support\n- other AI sites\n- automatic scheduled archival\n\nThat distinction should keep the first version small enough that we can actually **start extracting chats quickly**.\n\n---\n\n# 13. Acceptance test\n\nBefore I would trust this against the chats we actually care about, it needs to pass four increasingly ugly tests:\n\n```text\nTEST 1\nSmall chat\n~10 messages\n\nExpected:\nperfect extraction\n```\n\n```text\nTEST 2\nMedium chat\n100+ messages\n\nExpected:\nperfect extraction\n```\n\n```text\nTEST 3\nLarge virtualized chat\nhundreds of messages\n\nExpected:\ninternal extraction succeeds\nDOM virtualization does not affect archive\n```\n\n```text\nTEST 4\nOne of your enormous existing project chats\n\nExpected:\nCtrl+A fails to reproduce whole chat\nOUR ARCHIVE DOES\n```\n\nTest 4 is the one that actually matters.\n\n---\n\n# 14. Definition of success\n\nI want this written into the design because it prevents us from moving the goalposts:\n\n> **A capture is successful only when the extractor can produce a local archive containing the complete user-visible conversation independently of Chrome's native text-selection behavior, with sufficient metadata to establish ordering and identity and an integrity report describing how completeness was established.**\n\nThat is the core requirement.\n\n---\n\n## Decisions I consider locked\n\n| Question | Decision |\n|---|---|\n| Depend on Ctrl+A? | **No** |\n| Depend on highlighting? | **No** |\n| Selection recorder? | Yes, secondary feature |\n| Primary capture | Authenticated internal conversation fetch |\n| Fallback | DOM hydration/recorder |\n| Persistent capture | Yes |\n| Resume interrupted captures | Yes |\n| Canonical format | Structured JSON |\n| Human-readable format | Markdown |\n| Simple portable format | TXT |\n| Preserve branches | Yes |\n| Integrity hashes | Yes |\n| Completeness reporting | Yes |\n| External servers | **None** |\n| Telemetry | **None** |\n| API key required | **No** |\n| Save auth tokens | **No** |\n| Hidden system/reasoning extraction | **No** |\n| Initial browser | Chromium/Chrome |\n| Initial target | One open ChatGPT chat |\n\nThat is enough of a design baseline to begin implementation without having Codex make architectural decisions for us.\n\nThe next engineering step is therefore **not more brainstorming**. It is to establish the repository, put this specification under version control, define the canonical JSON schema and acceptance tests, and build the smallest possible extractor against a disposable conversation before pointing it at any important archive. Given how you have been handling these projects, I would put the build under the same governed Git/GACP workflow rather than letting the implementation become another undocumented browser script. memcite"

            "Yes. This is small enough that **we do not need Codex for the initial build**, and I would avoid disrupting the CICS reconciliation for it.\n\nThe MVP is basically a compact Manifest V3 Chrome extension with perhaps 6–10 files:\n\n- `manifest.json`\n- content script\n- page-side conversation extractor\n- service worker/local persistence\n- normalizer\n- export code\n- small popup/UI\n- tests/fixtures\n- design/schema documentation\n\nI can design the individual files here, give you exact terminal commands to create them on the Steam Deck, review the resulting output/errors, and iterate with you interactively. We don't need an autonomous coding agent to manage that amount of code.\n\nThere is actually an advantage to doing **v0.1 without Codex**: we are dealing with an undocumented ChatGPT interface. During initial reverse-engineering, we're probably going to do a lot of:\n\n```text\ninstall unpacked extension\n→ open test chat\n→ inspect result\n→ \"okay, OpenAI structures this field this way\"\n→ adjust extractor\n→ reload extension\n→ test again\n```\n\nYou are sitting at the browser and can immediately tell me what happened. That feedback loop is arguably better than throwing a large implementation prompt at Codex and having it make assumptions.\n\nI would use Codex later when we reach things like automated tests, schema migrations, large refactors, DOM-fallback hardening, Firefox support, batch extraction, or integration with your larger archival/project-recovery system. At that point it becomes useful parallel engineering capacity.\n\nSo I recommend:\n\n**Keep Codex working on CICS. Build the Chat Archive Extractor with me directly.**\n\nAnd still put it in Git from the first commit so we're not creating another orphan script.\n\nI would start with an intentionally tiny milestone:\n\n> **v0.0.1 — prove that we can open one ChatGPT conversation and obtain its complete structured conversation data despite DOM virtualization.**\n\nNo UI, no IndexedDB, no Markdown exporter yet. Just prove the critical bypass works.\n\nIf that works on one of your giant chats, then we know the entire project is technically viable before spending effort building everything around it. memcite"

          "parts": [
            "Yes, it is possible to make **something** useful with a 3B model, but for **your specific PEIS use case** I would treat 3B as a **debugging / baseline model**, not the target operating model.\n\nWhy:\n\n- Qwen2.5 3B is a real instruction-tuned model and Ollama exposes it as a supported local option, so it is valid for basic structured generation and narrow tasks. The official model materials describe Qwen2.5 3B Instruct as a 3.09B instruction model, and Ollama lists Qwen2.5 sizes from 0.5B through 72B. citeturn957132search0turn957132search2\n- Your direct curl test already showed the 3B model can return the required JSON for a tiny constrained prompt in about 10 seconds total. That means the model is not categorically unusable; it is just not yet proving reliable on the **full PEIS planning prompt path**.\n- PEIS planning, even in its current narrow form, is not a trivial one-shot completion. It involves prompt-pack construction, retrieval grounding, JSON discipline, and robustness under vague real-world inputs. That is exactly the kind of workload where a 7B model usually gives a better margin for instruction-following and stability than a 3B model.\n\nMy recommendation:\n\n- **Yes, consider a 7B.**\n- Do **not** switch models yet as a substitute for diagnosis.\n- First, capture and test the exact PEIS-built prompt against 3B.\n- Then test the **same exact prompt** against 7B.\n\nThat gives you a clean answer:\n- if 3B fails and 7B succeeds, then 7B is the practical floor for this workflow\n- if both fail, the problem is prompt construction/integration, not model size\n- if both succeed but only PEIS times out, the issue is in your runtime path\n\nOperationally, I would frame it this way:\n\n- **3B**: acceptable for smoke tests, deterministic scaffolding checks, tiny JSON tasks\n- **7B**: much more plausible as the first model size for a PEIS planner you might actually trust\n- **14B+**: worth considering later if you want broader, messier planning inputs with less brittle prompting\n\nOne important detail: the official Qwen2.5 and Ollama materials advertise long context support, but advertised context length does **not** mean a small model will handle large grounded prompts well in practice. Context capacity and practical planning reliability are not the same thing. citeturn957132search0turn957132search2turn957132search6\n\nMy judgment from what you’ve shown so far:\n\n**A 3B can help you debug PEIS. A 7B is a much more credible candidate for making PEIS actually usable.**\n\nThe clean next test would be to pull `qwen2.5:7b` and run the exact captured PEIS prompt against both models."

truncation\n  - summarization\n  - token budgeting\n  - field filtering\n\nFor a 3B or 7B local model, that can easily:\n\n- slow prompt eval massively\n- cause long internal chain-of-thought style wandering\n- blow practical latency even if not hitting hard context limit\n\n## Key point\n\nThis is not a PEIS architecture failure.\n\nThis is a **normal first-generation local RAG prompt mistake**:\n\n> feeding too much raw artifact structure into a small model.\n\nThat is fixable.\n\n## Shortest path to usefulness now\n\nDo NOT redesign retrieval.\n\nDo NOT add embeddings.\n\nDo NOT expand scope.\n\nDo this:\n\n## Step 1: Prove prompt size\n\nIn `src/peis/planning/draft.py`, right before:\n\n```python\nraw_output = model_invoke_fn(prompt)\n```\n\nadd:\n\n```python\nprint(f\"PROMPT LENGTH: {len(prompt)}\")\nwith open(\"/tmp/peis_prompt.txt\", \"w\") as f:\n    f.write(prompt)\n```\n\nRun:\n\n```bash\n.venv/bin/python peis_planning_smoke.py\n```\n\nEven if it times out, the prompt file should be written.\n\nThen run:\n\n```bash\nwc -c /tmp/peis_prompt.txt\n```\n\nand:\n\n```bash\nhead -100 /tmp/peis_prompt.txt\n```\n\nPaste both.\n\n## Step 2: Immediate likely fix (after confirming)\n\nMost likely first real fix:\n\n### change retrieval max_examples from 3 → 1\n\nIn `retrieval.py`:\n\n```python\ndef build_grounding_context(..., max_examples: int = 1)\n```\n\nThis alone may solve it.\n\n### better:\ntruncate examples to only:\n\n- objective\n- step action types\n\ninstead of dumping full artifacts.\n\nBut first:\n\n## do not guess\n\nMeasure prompt length first.\n\nThat is now the shortest path to getting PEIS planning unstuck."

            "from __future__ import annotations\n\nfrom typing import Any, Dict, List\n\nfrom .artifact_store import ArtifactStore\n\n\nclass RetrievalError(ValueError):\n    pass\n\n\nclass PlanningRetrieval:\n    \"\"\"\n    Retrieval layer for planning grounding.\n\n    Pulls prior artifacts and selects relevant examples\n    to inject into prompt construction.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self, store: ArtifactStore):\n        self.store = store\n\n    # -------------------------\n    # PUBLIC API\n    # -------------------------\n\n    def build_grounding_context(\n        self,\n        objective: str,\n        max_examples: int = 3,\n    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Build structured grounding context for prompt injection.\n        \"\"\"\n\n        validated = self.store.get_validated_plans()\n        failures = self.store.get_failure_cases()\n        corrections = self.store.get_correction_cases()\n\n        return {\n            \"validated_examples\": self._select_validated(validated, objective, max_examples),\n            \"failure_examples\": self._select_failures(failures, max_examples),\n            \"correction_examples\": self._select_corrections(corrections, max_examples),\n        }\n\n    # -------------------------\n    # SELECTION LOGIC\n    # -------------------------\n\n    def _select_validated(\n        self,\n        items: List[Dict[str, Any]],\n        objective: str,\n        k: int,\n    ) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Naive relevance: keyword overlap on objective.\n        Deterministic.\n        \"\"\"\n\n        scored = []\n\n        for item in items:\n            plan_obj = item.get(\"plan\", {}).get(\"objective\", \"\")\n            score = self._overlap_score(objective, plan_obj)\n            scored.append((score, item))\n\n        scored.sort(key=lambda x: (-x[0], self._stable_id(x[1])))\n\n        return [x[1] for x in scored[:k]]\n\n    def _select_failures(\n        self,\n        items: List[Dict[str, Any]],\n        k: int,\n    ) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Select most recent failures (deterministic ordering via ID).\n        \"\"\"\n\n        items_sorted = sorted(items, key=self._stable_id)\n        return items_sorted[-k:]\n\n    def _select_corrections(\n        self,\n        items: List[Dict[str, Any]],\n        k: int,\n    ) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Select corrections (prefer diversity via ID ordering).\n        \"\"\"\n\n        items_sorted = sorted(items, key=self._stable_id)\n        return items_sorted[:k]\n\n    # -------------------------\n    # UTIL\n    # -------------------------\n\n    def _overlap_score(self, a: str, b: str) -> int:\n        a_set = set(a.lower().split())\n        b_set = set(b.lower().split())\n        return len(a_set.intersection(b_set))\n\n    def _stable_id(self, item: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:\n        for key in [\n            \"validated_plan_id\",\n            \"failure_case_id\",\n            \"correction_case_id\",\n        ]:\n            if key in item:\n                return item[key]\n        return \"\"\n\nfull replacements ONLY"

            "That result is clear.\n\nReducing example count from 3 to 1 cut prompt length from **8282** to **5648**, but the call still timed out at the exact same Ollama step.\n\nSo:\n\n- grounding volume **is part of the problem**\n- but **example count alone is not enough**\n- the remaining blocker is the **content shape** of the grounding, not just the count\n\nThe prompt is still carrying too much irrelevant structure:\n- full session snapshots\n- determinism envelopes\n- timestamps\n- raw validation payloads\n- nested artifact metadata\n\nThat needs to be compacted, not merely reduced.\n\n## Next exact move\n\nKeep retrieval at `max_examples=1`, but change retrieval to return **minimal example objects** instead of full artifacts.\n\nYou want each example reduced to the smallest useful learning signal.\n\nUse this as the full replacement for `src/peis/planning/retrieval.py`:\n\n```python\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nfrom typing import Any, Dict, List\n\nfrom .artifact_store import ArtifactStore\n\n\nclass RetrievalError(ValueError):\n    pass\n\n\nclass PlanningRetrieval:\n    \"\"\"\n    Retrieval layer for planning grounding.\n\n    Pulls prior artifacts and selects relevant examples\n    to inject into prompt construction.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self, store: ArtifactStore):\n        self.store = store\n\n    # -------------------------\n    # PUBLIC API\n    # -------------------------\n\n    def build_grounding_context(\n        self,\n        objective: str,\n        max_examples: int = 1,\n    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Build structured grounding context for prompt injection.\n        \"\"\"\n\n        validated = self.store.get_validated_plans()\n        failures = self.store.get_failure_cases()\n        corrections = self.store.get_correction_cases()\n\n        selected_validated = self._select_validated(validated, objective, max_examples)\n        selected_failures = self._select_failures(failures, max_examples)\n        selected_corrections = self._select_corrections(corrections, max_examples)\n\n        return {\n            \"validated_examples\": [\n                self._compact_validated_example(item) for item in selected_validated\n            ],\n            \"failure_examples\": [\n                self._compact_failure_example(item) for item in selected_failures\n            ],\n            \"correction_examples\": [\n                self._compact_correction_example(item) for item in selected_corrections\n            ],\n        }\n\n    # -------------------------\n    # SELECTION LOGIC\n    # -------------------------\n\n    def _select_validated(\n        self,\n        items: List[Dict[str, Any]],\n        objective: str,\n        k: int,\n    ) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Naive relevance: keyword overlap on objective.\n        Deterministic.\n        \"\"\"\n\n        scored = []\n\n        for item in items:\n            plan_obj = item.get(\"plan\", {}).get(\"objective\", \"\")\n            score = self._overlap_score(objective, plan_obj)\n            scored.append((score, item))\n\n        scored.sort(key=lambda x: (-x[0], self._stable_id(x[1])))\n        return [x[1] for x in scored[:k]]\n\n    def _select_failures(\n        self,\n        items: List[Dict[str, Any]],\n        k: int,\n    ) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Select most recent failures (deterministic ordering via ID).\n        \"\"\"\n\n        items_sorted = sorted(items, key=self._stable_id)\n        return items_sorted[-k:]\n\n    def _select_corrections(\n        self,\n        items: List[Dict[str, Any]],\n        k: int,\n    ) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Select corrections (prefer diversity via ID ordering).\n        \"\"\"\n\n        items_sorted = sorted(items, key=self._stable_id)\n        return items_sorted[:k]\n\n    # -------------------------\n    # COMPACTION\n    # -------------------------\n\n    def _compact_validated_example(self, item: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        plan = item.get(\"plan\", {})\n        return {\n            \"objective\": plan.get(\"objective\", \"\"),\n            \"steps\": self._extract_steps(plan.get(\"steps\", [])),\n        }\n\n    def _compact_failure_example(self, item: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        normalized_output = item.get(\"normalized_output\", \"\")\n        return {\n            \"failure_type\": item.get(\"failure_type\", \"\"),\n            \"validation_errors\": item.get(\"validation_errors\", []),\n            \"raw_output\": normalized_output if isinstance(normalized_output, str) else \"\",\n        }\n\n    def _compact_correction_example(self, item: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        validation_result = item.get(\"validation_result\", {})\n        corrected_plan = validation_result.get(\"plan\", {})\n\n        return {\n            \"correction_type\": item.get(\"correction_type\", \"\"),\n            \"corrected_objective\": corrected_plan.get(\"objective\", \"\"),\n            \"corrected_steps\": self._extract_steps(corrected_plan.get(\"steps\", [])),\n        }\n\n    def _extract_steps(self, steps: Any) -> List[Dict[str, str]]:\n        if not isinstance(steps, list):\n            return []\n\n        compact_steps: List[Dict[str, str]] = []\n\n        for step in steps:\n            if not isinstance(step, dict):\n                continue\n\n            action_type = step.get(\"action_type\")\n            if isinstance(action_type, str) and action_type.strip():\n                compact_steps.append({\"action_type\": action_type.strip()})\n\n        return compact_steps\n\n    # -------------------------\n    # UTIL\n    # -------------------------\n\n    def _overlap_score(self, a: str, b: str) -> int:\n        a_set = set(a.lower().split())\n        b_set = set(b.lower().split())\n        return len(a_set.intersection(b_set))\n\n    def _stable_id(self, item: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:\n        for key in [\n            \"validated_plan_id\",\n            \"failure_case_id\",\n            \"correction_case_id\",\n        ]:\n            if key in item:\n                return item[key]\n        return \"\"\n```\n\nThen rerun:\n\n```bash\n.venv/bin/python peis_planning_smoke.py\n```\n\nWhat I expect:\n- prompt length should drop sharply again\n- if it still times out after this, the next target is the **objective/prompt wording** rather than grounding payload size"

          "content_type": "text",
          "parts": [
            "The bug is exactly where expected.\n\n## Root cause\n\n`runtime.py` always reports:\n\n```python\n\"validation_status\": result.get(\"validation_result\", {}).get(\"status\")\n```\n\nBut in an adjudicated success case:\n\n- `result[\"status\"]` = final repaired status (`VALID`)\n- `result[\"validation_result\"]` = original failed draft validation (`INVALID`)\n- `result[\"adjudicated_validation_result\"]` = final repaired validation (`VALID`)\n\nSo the UI meta is incorrectly showing the draft status instead of the final status. fileciteturn4file0\n\n## Smallest correct fix\n\nFix only normalization logic.\nDo not touch recovery flow.\n\n## Full replacement for `src/peis/planning/runtime.py`\n\n```python\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nfrom typing import Any, Callable, Dict\n\nfrom peis.planning.artifact_store import ArtifactStore\nfrom peis.planning.recover import run_recovery_pipeline\n\n\nclass PEISRuntimeError(RuntimeError):\n    pass\n\n\nclass PlanningRuntime:\n    \"\"\"\n    Entry point for PEIS planning system.\n\n    This is the ONLY interface that external systems (Open WebUI, local AI, etc.)\n    should call.\n\n    It enforces:\n    - full pipeline execution\n    - adjudication loop\n    - artifact persistence\n    - deterministic boundaries\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(\n        self,\n        *,\n        artifact_store: ArtifactStore,\n        model_invoke_fn: Callable[[str], str],\n        adjudicate_fn: Callable[[Dict[str, Any]], str],\n    ):\n        self.artifact_store = artifact_store\n        self.model_invoke_fn = model_invoke_fn\n        self.adjudicate_fn = adjudicate_fn\n\n    # -------------------------\n    # PUBLIC API\n    # -------------------------\n\n    def run(\n        self,\n        *,\n        planning_request: Dict[str, Any],\n        session_snapshot: Dict[str, Any],\n    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Execute full planning lifecycle.\n\n        This is what your UI calls.\n        \"\"\"\n\n        self._validate_inputs(planning_request, session_snapshot)\n\n        result = run_recovery_pipeline(\n            planning_request=planning_request,\n            session_snapshot=session_snapshot,\n            model_invoke_fn=self.model_invoke_fn,\n            adjudicate_fn=self.adjudicate_fn,\n            artifact_store=self.artifact_store,\n        )\n\n        return self._normalize_output(result)\n\n    # -------------------------\n    # INTERNALS\n    # -------------------------\n\n    def _validate_inputs(\n        self,\n        planning_request: Dict[str, Any],\n        session_snapshot: Dict[str, Any],\n    ) -> None:\n        if not isinstance(planning_request, dict):\n            raise PEISRuntimeError(\"planning_request must be a dict\")\n\n        if not isinstance(session_snapshot, dict):\n            raise PEISRuntimeError(\"session_snapshot must be a dict\")\n\n        if \"objective\" not in planning_request:\n            raise PEISRuntimeError(\"planning_request must include 'objective'\")\n\n        if \"determinism_envelope\" not in session_snapshot:\n            raise PEISRuntimeError(\n                \"session_snapshot must include determinism_envelope\"\n            )\n\n    def _normalize_output(self, result: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        \"\"\"\n        Normalize runtime output for UI consumption.\n\n        This is the ONLY place allowed to reshape output.\n        \"\"\"\n\n        had_adjudication = result.get(\"adjudicated_output\") is not None\n\n        if had_adjudication:\n            final_validation_status = (\n                result.get(\"adjudicated_validation_result\", {}).get(\"status\")\n            )\n        else:\n            final_validation_status = (\n                result.get(\"validation_result\", {}).get(\"status\")\n            )\n\n        return {\n            \"status\": result[\"status\"],\n            \"plan\": result.get(\"validated_plan\"),\n            \"escalation_required\": result.get(\"escalation_required\", False),\n            \"hard_fail\": result.get(\"hard_fail\", False),\n            \"meta\": {\n                \"had_adjudication\": had_adjudication,\n                \"validation_status\": final_validation_status,\n            },\n        }\n```"

[L2]   "content": "# PEIS Environment Design

- Conversation ID: `69c9e242-3c84-83e8-892b-6d71f5fdb7b9`
- Exported: 2026-08-25T19:44:32.969Z
- Scope: human-visible user/assistant messages on the active conversation branch

---

## User

PEIS IMPLEMENTATION STATUS: COMPLETE

I have built a deterministic, governed execution system with:
- PlanRecord → Executor → CapabilityRegistry → ExecutionResultRecord → Storage
- CLI entrypoint working
- End-to-end execution verified
- 149/149 tests passing

I also have:
- Open WebUI running locally
- local model (qwen2.5:3b)
- ChatGPT as reasoning layer

PROBLEM:
My local model requires manual correction to produce valid PEIS plans.
This is inefficient and not scalable.

OBJECTIVE:
Design a persistent environment where:
- local model is pre-grounded in PEIS (no hallucinated domains)
- capability inventory is known automatically
- outputs are constrained to PEIS-valid plans
- ChatGPT refines but does not babysit every step
- minimal manual correction is required

CONSTRAINTS:
- PEIS architecture is already correct — do not redesign it
- focus only on environment + orchestration + prompt grounding
- system must remain deterministic and governed

Start by asking only the necessary questions to remove ambiguity.

## Assistant

Only these questions matter before locking the environment design:

1. **Where will the grounding live?**  
Do you want the local model grounded primarily through:
- a **retrieval context layer** from PEIS artifacts/docs,
- a **strict system prompt / role contract**,
- a **schema-constrained generation layer**,
- or all three, with a defined precedence order?

2. **What are the authoritative inputs for plan generation?**  
Which exact artifacts should be treated as canonical at generation time?
For example:
- capability registry manifest
- action type schema / plan schema
- policy snapshot
- examples of valid PlanRecord artifacts
- execution history / prior successful plans

3. **How dynamic is the capability inventory?**  
Should the environment assume capability inventory is:
- effectively static and rebuilt only on deploy,
- refreshed on startup,
- or refreshed before each planning session?

4. **What is the local model allowed to do?**  
Should qwen be responsible for:
- generating the full candidate plan,
- generating only a structured draft to be validated and repaired,
- or selecting from pre-authored action templates plus parameters?

5. **What is ChatGPT’s exact role boundary?**  
When you say “refines but does not babysit,” should ChatGPT:
- only critique/rewrite invalid local-model plans,
- act as a second-pass planner,
- or only intervene on failure / ambiguity / halt states?

6. **What is the desired failure behavior?**  
If the local model cannot produce a PEIS-valid plan, should the environment:
- hard-fail,
- auto-repair through deterministic validators/rewriters,
- escalate to ChatGPT,
- or fall back to a restricted template-based planner?

7. **What surfaces are already available inside Open WebUI?**  
Do you currently have, or intend to add:
- tool/function calling,
- retrieval/RAG hooks,
- custom system prompts per model,
- workflow/pipeline nodes,
- or only plain chat with model-specific prompts?

8. **What should be persisted across sessions?**  
Which of these must be durable:
- PEIS grounding corpus
- capability inventory snapshot
- prompt pack / role contract
- prior validated plans
- failure cases and correction examples

9. **What is the unit of determinism for this environment?**  
Should a planning session bind to a fixed snapshot of:
- capability inventory
- policy snapshot
- grounding corpus version
- model version
- prompt pack version
so that the same request under the same inputs should yield the same validated plan envelope?

10. **Do you want the local model prevented from free-form domain invention by architecture, or just strongly discouraged?**  
In other words, should invalid action domains be:
- impossible via constrained decoding / structured selection,
- or merely rejected after generation?

Once you answer those, the design can be pinned without touching PEIS architecture.

## User

Use this as the lock:

Where grounding lives
All three, with this precedence:
schema-constrained generation layer
strict system prompt / role contract
retrieval context layer from PEIS artifacts/docs

Reason: schema and allowed action surface must dominate prompt wording, and prompt must dominate retrieved prose.

Authoritative inputs for plan generation
Canonical inputs at generation time:
capability inventory manifest
action type / plan schema
current policy snapshot
prompt pack / role contract version
small curated set of valid PlanRecord examples
recent successful execution artifacts only when relevant

Do not treat raw execution history broadly as authoritative. Only curated examples and explicitly referenced prior successful plans.

Capability inventory dynamism
Refresh on startup and bind that snapshot for the session.

Not per deploy only. Not before every single prompt unless startup state changed.

What the local model is allowed to do
Generate a structured draft to be validated and repaired.

Not full trusted plan generation.
Not pure template selection only.

So qwen is the drafting layer, not the authority layer.

ChatGPT role boundary
Second-pass planner and validator, but not constant babysitter.

Exact role:

review qwen draft
repair invalid structure or capability misuse
tighten into PEIS-valid plan envelope
intervene directly on ambiguity, failure, or halt conditions

So ChatGPT is the adjudicating planner, not the first drafter every time.

Desired failure behavior
Ordered behavior:
deterministic validator/rewriter attempts repair
if still invalid, escalate to ChatGPT
if still invalid, hard-fail

Do not silently fall back to freeform behavior.
Do not let qwen output execute unvalidated.

Open WebUI surfaces
Assume only:
plain chat
model-specific/system prompts

Treat anything else as optional future enhancement until explicitly verified in that environment.

What persists across sessions
Must be durable:
capability inventory snapshot
prompt pack / role contract
PEIS grounding corpus
prior validated plans

User asks for work. The environment normalizes that request into a stable internal planning input.

- `ESCALATE_CHATGPT`
- `HARD_FAIL`

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
from typing import Any, Mapping


class AuthorityError(ValueError):
    """Raised when authority rules are violated."""


class AuthorityClass(str, Enum):
    """
    System-wide authority classes.

    These classes are intentionally narrow and explicit. Any object that can
    influence interpretation, explanation, routing, or decision-making should
    be assigned exactly one authority class.
    """

    AUTHORITATIVE = "authoritative"
    DERIVED_AUTHORITATIVE = "derived_authoritative"
    ADVISORY = "advisory"

    and an authoritative decision artifact may both be authoritative, but they
    play different roles in the system.

class AuthorityBinding:

    - Every bound object has exactly one authority class.

    become decision-driving merely because such references are attached.
    """
    return AuthorityBinding(
        authority_class=AuthorityClass.ADVISORY,
        evidence_role=evidence_role,
        evidence_snapshot_id=evidence_snapshot_id,
        policy_snapshot_id=policy_snapshot_id,
        source_label=source_label,

    *,
    evidence_role: EvidenceRole,
    source_label: str,

    policy_snapshot_id: str | None = None,

        evidence_role=evidence_role,

    if not isinstance(binding, AuthorityBinding):

    if not binding.is_decision_authoritative:

    if not isinstance(binding, AuthorityBinding):

    if not binding.is_non_authoritative:

            f"non-authoritative: {binding.authority_class.value}"

    left: AuthorityBinding,
    right: AuthorityBinding,

    Ties are structural and therefore invalid to resolve here.

    if not isinstance(right, AuthorityBinding):
        raise AuthorityError("right must be an AuthorityBinding")

    left_rank = _authority_rank(left.authority_class)
    right_rank = _authority_rank(right.authority_class)

    if left_rank > right_rank:
        return left
    if right_rank > left_rank:
        return right

    raise AuthorityError(
        "cannot resolve equal-authority bindings without domain-specific rules: "
        f"{left.authority_class.value}"
    )


def assert_no_descriptive_decision_input(bindings: list[AuthorityBinding]) -> None:
    """
    Hard-fail if any descriptive binding is presented as decision input.
    """
    for binding in bindings:
        if not isinstance(binding, AuthorityBinding):
            raise AuthorityError("all bindings must be AuthorityBinding instances")
        if binding.authority_class == AuthorityClass.DESCRIPTIVE:
            raise AuthorityError(
                "descriptive data must not be used as decision input"
            )


def assert_no_advisory_decision_input(bindings: list[AuthorityBinding]) -> None:
    """
    Hard-fail if any advisory binding is presented as decision input.
    """
    for binding in bindings:
        if not isinstance(binding, AuthorityBinding):
            raise AuthorityError("all bindings must be AuthorityBinding instances")
        if binding.authority_class == AuthorityClass.ADVISORY:
            raise AuthorityError(
                "advisory data must not be used as decision input"
            )


def _authority_rank(authority_class: AuthorityClass) -> int:
    """
    Internal total ordering for authority resolution.
    """
    match authority_class:
        case AuthorityClass.AUTHORITATIVE:
            return 4
        case AuthorityClass.DERIVED_AUTHORITATIVE:
            return 3
        case AuthorityClass.ADVISORY:
            return 2
        case AuthorityClass.DESCRIPTIVE:
            return 1

    raise AuthorityError(f"unsupported authority class: {authority_class!r}")


def _coerce_enum[T: Enum](
    enum_cls: type[T],
    value: Any,
    *,
    field_name: str,
) -> T:
    if isinstance(value, enum_cls):
        return value

    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
        raise AuthorityError(f"{field_name} must be a non-empty string")

    normalized = value.strip()
    try:
        return enum_cls(normalized)
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise AuthorityError(
            f"{field_name} has unsupported value: {normalized!r}"
        ) from exc

    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
        raise AuthorityError(f"{field_name} must be a non-empty string")
    return value.strip()


def _coerce_optional_str(value: Any, *, field_name: str) -> str | None:
    if value is None:
        return None
    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
        raise AuthorityError(f"{field_name} must be None or a non-empty string")
    return value.strip()


def _require_non_empty_str(value: str | None, *, field_name: str) -> None:
    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
        raise AuthorityError(f"{field_name} must be a non-empty string")

    UNKNOWN = "UNKNOWN"
    UNKNOWN_PENDING = "UNKNOWN_PENDING"
    BLOCKED_HUMAN = "BLOCKED_HUMAN"
    CONFLICT = "CONFLICT"
    HALT_CONFLICT = "HALT_CONFLICT"
    HALT_STRUCTURAL = "HALT_STRUCTURAL"

    {
        StopState.RESOLVED,
        StopState.UNKNOWN,
        StopState.BLOCKED_HUMAN,
        StopState.CONFLICT,
        StopState.HALT_CONFLICT,
        StopState.HALT_STRUCTURAL,
    }
)

_HALT_STATES: frozenset[StopState] = frozenset(
    {
        StopState.HALT_CONFLICT,
        StopState.HALT_STRUCTURAL,
    }
)

_NON_TERMINAL_STATES: frozenset[StopState] = frozenset(
    {
        StopState.UNKNOWN_PENDING,
    }
)

    Immutable stop-state decision artifact.

    Required invariants:
    - Every decision must declare exactly one authoritative stop-state.

    - Halt states may not be marked resumable within the same decision artifact.

        _require_non_empty_str(

        )

            field_name="policy_snapshot_id",

            _require_non_empty_str(self.details, field_name="details")

                "halt states may not be marked resumable in the same decision"

    def is_terminal(self) -> bool:

        return is_terminal_state(self.stop_state)

    @property
    def is_halt(self) -> bool:
        """Return True when this decision is a halt condition."""
        return is_halt_state(self.stop_state)

    def requires_human_intervention(self) -> bool:
